technique: **PICO family (population, intervention, comparison, outcome; variants PICOT, PEO, PICo, SPIDER)**
what_it_does: Splits a vague topic into named slots. Artefact: a one-sentence structured question and a slot table. An empty or vague slot shows the question is not yet researchable. PICOT adds type of study; PEO (population, exposure, outcome) replaces the intervention with an exposure; PICo (population, phenomenon of interest, context) and SPIDER (sample, phenomenon of interest, design, evaluation, research type) suit qualitative questions.
fit_test: No comparator exists or the outcome cannot be observed (switch to PEO, PICo or SPIDER). Designed for health and social science and not tested for policy or business topics.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described in library guides only; no evidence found that using it improves review quality. ([Jefferson library guide, PICO variations](https://jefflibraries.libguides.com/PICO/Variations))
purpose: Splits a vague topic into named slots (population, intervention or exposure, comparison, outcome) and produces a one-sentence structured question and a slot table.
use_when: Use when the topic is vague and you need a researchable question about an intervention, an exposure or an experience.
requires_minimum: A topic stated in at least one sentence and a view on whether it concerns an intervention, an exposure or an experience.
not_for_text: No comparator exists or the outcome cannot be observed, in which case a variant such as PEO, PICo or SPIDER fits better. It was designed for health and social science and is untested for policy or business topics.
related_techniques: pairs with :: FQ-03 :: Working definitions for each slot term remove ambiguity inside the slots; pairs with :: FQ-06 :: Criteria checking confirms the structured question has a measure and a time limit
typical_model_failure: Fills an empty slot with a plausible invention instead of reporting that the slot cannot be filled from the topic.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Indirectness if the topic is not about an intervention, exposure or experience; the technique shapes the question and does not test any claim, so certainty depends on later techniques.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result gives a one-sentence structured question and a slot table with one row per slot (population, intervention or exposure, comparison, outcome, or the slots of the variant used), each row holding the content of that slot. It marks any slot that is empty or vague and states whether that means the question is not yet researchable.

technique: **Decision-first framing (decision-focused or value-focused question design)**
what_it_does: Starts from the decision to be made and works back to the evidence that would change it. Artefact: a list of questions, each tagged with the option it could change. Questions that change no option are out of scope.
fit_test: No decision exists (pure description), or a 'yes' and a 'no' answer lead to the same action.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** No source was retrieved. The note author treats it as practice with a decision analysis background that was not verified.
purpose: Starts from the decision to be made and works back to a list of questions, each tagged with the option it could change.
use_when: Use when a decision is pending and you want to ask only the questions whose answers could change which option is chosen.
requires_minimum: The decision, its options and the decision maker criteria.
not_for_text: No decision exists (pure description), or a yes answer and a no answer lead to the same action.
related_techniques: pairs with :: DM-01 :: An issue tree can split the decision question into sub-questions; pairs with :: FQ-06 :: Criteria checking confirms each retained question has a measure and a time limit
typical_model_failure: Invents decision options or decision criteria that the decision maker has not stated.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Risk of bias if the decision maker states the options or criteria incompletely; indirectness if the question list drifts from the actual decision.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a list of questions, each tagged with the option it could change. It names the decision the questions serve and lists separately the questions that change no option and are therefore out of scope.

technique: **Definitional analysis (explication, concept clarification, conceptual analysis)**
what_it_does: Replaces ambiguous key terms with precise working definitions before the question is asked. Artefact: a glossary with borderline cases; the borderline cases mark where answers will differ by definition.
fit_test: Two analysts applying the definition to one case disagree, or the definition is circular or excludes clear cases.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** The Stanford Encyclopedia confirms that Carnap replaced 'rational reconstruction' with 'explication'. Carnap's four requirements and critiques such as the paradox of analysis were not confirmed. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Carnap](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/carnap/))
purpose: Replaces ambiguous key terms with precise working definitions and produces a glossary with borderline cases.
use_when: Use when the key terms of the question mean different things to different people and answers could differ by definition.
requires_minimum: The key terms of the question and at least two examples of how each is used.
not_for_text: Two analysts applying a definition to one case disagree, or the definition is circular or excludes clear cases.
related_techniques: pairs with :: FQ-01 :: Defined terms make the slots of a structured question unambiguous; pairs with :: FQ-04 :: A reversal between frames may come from a term used in two senses
typical_model_failure: Supplies a dictionary definition for a contested term and does not test it against borderline cases.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Indirectness if a definition is chosen to favour a conclusion; the borderline cases carry the uncertainty and should be reported with the definitions.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a glossary with one entry per ambiguous key term, giving the precise working definition. Each entry lists its borderline cases, and the result names the borderline cases where answers would differ by definition.

technique: **Reframing and issue redefinition (changing the level of analysis or baseline; five-step issue redefinition)**
what_it_does: Restates the question at another level (individual, organisation, system), with another baseline, or by rephrasing, broadening, narrowing and reversing it. Artefact: answers side by side; an answer that reverses between frames depends on wording.
fit_test: The alternative frames differ only in wording. A reversal between frames is a finding about the topic, not a failure of the technique.
status_and_evidence: **Practice.** The framing effect is documented in psychology (in the Asian disease problem, 72 per cent chose the certain option when outcomes were framed as lives saved and 78 per cent chose the risky option when framed as deaths) ([Wikipedia, Framing effect (psychology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framing_effect_(psychology))). Deliberate reframing as a research technique was not sourced; issue redefinition is named in the UK handbook ([UK Red Teaming Handbook](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1027158/20210625-Red_Teaming_Handbook.pdf)).
purpose: Restates the question at another level, with another baseline, or by rephrasing, broadening, narrowing and reversing it, and produces answers side by side.
use_when: Use when the answer may depend on how the question is worded or at what level it is asked.
requires_minimum: The current framing and at least one alternative framing.
not_for_text: The alternative frames differ only in wording. A reversal between frames is a finding about the topic, not a failure of the technique.
related_techniques: pairs with :: FQ-05 :: Several explicit models test whether the answer depends on the model as well as the wording; pairs with :: DM-16 :: Levels of analysis give a defined set of levels for the reframing
typical_model_failure: Produces frames that differ only in wording, so that the answers agree for a trivial reason.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Inconsistency is reported when answers reverse between frames; limited evidence that deliberate reframing improves research quality.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result states the question in each frame used (such as individual, organisation and system level, a different baseline, or a rephrased, broadened, narrowed or reversed form) and places the answer to each frame side by side. It names the answers that reverse between frames and says that these depend on wording.

technique: **Multiple mental models (applying explicit models from several fields to one topic)**
what_it_does: Reads the same topic through several explicit models. Artefact: one reading per model; divergences mark areas of uncertainty.
fit_test: A model is applied outside its domain, or models are chosen after the answer is known.
status_and_evidence: **Practice.** Craik (1943) and Johnson-Laird (1983) are documented as psychological theory; the multidisciplinary use for decisions is practice with no effectiveness evidence found. ([Wikipedia, Mental model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_model))
purpose: Reads one topic through several explicit models from different fields and produces one reading per model.
use_when: Use when you suspect that a single view of the topic hides alternative explanations and want to see where models disagree.
requires_minimum: At least three models whose assumptions are stated.
not_for_text: A model is applied outside its domain, or models are chosen after the answer is known.
related_techniques: pairs with :: FQ-04 :: Reframing tests wording and level while multiple models test the assumptions behind the reading; pairs with :: DM-16 :: Levels of analysis give one set of models that differ by level
typical_model_failure: Applies a model by name only, repeating one common reading under several labels.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Indirectness when a model is used outside its domain; divergence between models lowers certainty by inconsistency, and model choice is a source of bias.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result has one reading of the topic for each explicit model applied, with the model named at the head of each reading. It ends with a list of the points where the readings diverge, marked as areas of uncertainty.

technique: **SMART check (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound)**
what_it_does: Checks that an objective or question names a scope, a measure, a feasible target and a time limit. Artefact: the draft rewritten with each criterion answered; a criterion that cannot be answered is a gap in the framing.
fit_test: The work is exploratory and no measure can be set in advance. It was designed for management objectives, so its use on research questions is an extension.
status_and_evidence: **Practice.** The source page reports criticism that the original lacks a clear theoretical basis and that evidence for specific goals is mixed. ([Wikipedia, SMART criteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMART_criteria))
purpose: Checks that an objective or question names a scope, a measure, a feasible target and a time limit, and produces the draft rewritten with each criterion answered.
use_when: Use when a goal or question is drafted and you want to confirm it can be measured and finished before work begins.
requires_minimum: A draft goal or question.
not_for_text: The work is exploratory and no measure can be set in advance. It was designed for management objectives, so its use on research questions is an extension.
related_techniques: should follow :: FQ-01 :: A structured question gives the draft that the criteria are applied to; pairs with :: FQ-02 :: Decision-first framing supplies the options that the measure must be able to separate
typical_model_failure: Rewrites the question so that every criterion appears answered when the target or time limit has been invented.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: The criteria test form, not whether the question is worth asking; invented targets lower certainty by indirectness.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is the draft objective or question rewritten with one answer for each of the five criteria: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Any criterion that cannot be answered is named as a gap in the framing.

technique: **MECE decomposition and issue tree (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive; logic tree, problem tree; related: work breakdown structure)**
what_it_does: Divides a topic into sub-parts that do not overlap and together cover the whole, repeated at each level. Artefact: a tree; read gaps (missing branches), overlaps and the relative size of branches.
fit_test: Items fit two branches, fit none, or an 'other' branch grows large. Wikipedia's example: grouping by nationality fails because some people hold two nationalities and some hold none.
status_and_evidence: **Practice.** Consulting practice attributed to Minto at McKinsey. Criticised as not fully exhaustive and as excluding useful redundancy; no effectiveness evidence found. ([Wikipedia, MECE principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MECE_principle))
purpose: Divides a topic into sub-parts that do not overlap and together cover the whole, repeated at each level, and produces a tree.
use_when: Use when a broad topic needs to be broken into non-overlapping parts so that gaps and overlaps in coverage become visible.
requires_minimum: One clearly stated topic and a splitting rule for each level.
not_for_text: Items fit two branches, fit none, or an other branch grows large. Grouping by nationality fails because some people hold two nationalities and some hold none.
related_techniques: pairs with :: DM-02 :: A hypothesis tree applies the same splitting to a claim and not a topic; pairs with :: FQ-02 :: A decision question gives the root of the tree
typical_model_failure: Produces a tree whose branches look exclusive but overlap, or that omits an awkward branch, while asserting that it is exhaustive.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Exhaustiveness cannot be proved; an other branch that grows lowers certainty by indirectness, and the splitting rule is a source of bias.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a tree with the topic at the top and sub-parts at each level, where the branches at each level do not overlap and together cover the parent. It names any gaps (missing branches), any overlaps, and the relative size of the branches.

technique: **Hypothesis tree (hypothesis-driven decomposition, claim decomposition)**
what_it_does: Splits a claim into the sub-claims that must all be true for it to be true. Artefact: a tree of claims; read leaf claims for which no evidence is possible.
fit_test: Leaves are vague, the parent can be true while every leaf is false, or the first hypothesis is kept after its top branch is refuted.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** No source was opened; two note files describe it from general knowledge only.
purpose: Splits a claim into the sub-claims that must all be true for it to be true and produces a tree of claims that goes into a claims register.
use_when: Use when a claim is too broad to test and you need to know which sub-claims need evidence.
requires_minimum: A claim and knowledge of what evidence would support or refute each branch.
not_for_text: Leaves are vague, the parent can be true while every leaf is false, or the first hypothesis is kept after its top branch is refuted.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-13 :: Competing hypotheses scoring rates evidence against hypotheses once the tree has defined them; pairs with :: TC1-16 :: A search for disconfirming evidence can be run on each leaf claim
typical_model_failure: Writes leaf claims that restate the parent in other words, so that no evidence could separate them.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Risk of bias because the split reflects the analyst view of what evidence is possible; the tree states what must be shown and does not show that it is true.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a tree in which the main claim is split into the sub-claims that must all be true for it to be true, down to leaf claims. It lists the leaf claims for which no evidence is possible.

technique: **Morphological analysis (Zwicky box, general morphological analysis)** Also serves: Project forward.
what_it_does: Lists the parameters of a topic and the possible values of each, then removes value pairs judged inconsistent. Artefact: a grid and a reduced set of consistent configurations; read values that appear in all or none.
fit_test: Almost all combinations are judged consistent, or almost none (parameters or values poorly defined), or the number of parameters makes the space too large to prune.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described as intended for non-quantified problems; consistency judgements are expert opinion; no accuracy evidence found. ([Wikipedia, Morphological analysis (problem-solving)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphological_analysis_(problem-solving)))
purpose: Lists the parameters of a topic and the possible values of each, removes value pairs judged inconsistent, and produces a grid and a reduced set of consistent configurations.
use_when: Use when a topic has several dimensions with discrete options and you need the set of workable combinations without numerical data.
requires_minimum: At least three parameters, each with at least two discrete values, and expert judgements of which value pairs are inconsistent.
not_for_text: Almost all combinations are judged consistent, or almost none, or the number of parameters makes the space too large to prune.
related_techniques: pairs with :: PJ-12 :: Consistent configurations can be written up as scenarios; pairs with :: PJ-13 :: A scenario matrix handles two axes where this technique handles many
typical_model_failure: Judges value pairs inconsistent from plausibility alone without recording the reasoning, so the reduced set cannot be audited.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:expert review; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; expert opinion; language model
certainty_limits: The consistency judgements are expert opinion with no accuracy evidence; they lower certainty by risk of bias and imprecision.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result has a grid with one column per parameter of the topic and the possible values of each listed under it, and a reduced set of consistent configurations after value pairs judged inconsistent are removed. It names the values that appear in all of the consistent configurations and the values that appear in none.

technique: **Value chain analysis (Porter)**
what_it_does: Divides a business unit's activities into five primary and four support activities. Artefact: a chain; read where cost and differentiation concentrate.
fit_test: Activities fit no listed category, as in services or platforms, which shows the manufacturing-derived structure is wrong. Porter advises business-unit level because higher levels hide advantage.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described on a secondary page citing Porter (1985); the page reports no criticisms, and criticisms for services and networks are unconfirmed. ([Wikipedia, Value chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_chain))
purpose: Divides the activities of one business unit into five primary and four support activities and produces a value chain showing where cost and differentiation concentrate.
use_when: Use when you want to see which activities of one business unit create cost or differentiation.
requires_minimum: The activities of one business unit, with costs and margins where available.
not_for_text: Activities fit no listed category, as in services or platforms, which shows the manufacturing-derived structure is wrong. Porter advises business-unit level because higher levels hide advantage.
consumes: charter or question:agreed; raw dataset or corpus:raw
related_techniques: pairs with :: DM-17 :: Process mapping gives the activity sequence that the chain summarises; pairs with :: CM1-12 :: Benchmarking compares activity costs with peers
typical_model_failure: Assigns activities to the nine categories from general knowledge and invents activity-level costs that are not published.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Imprecision because activity-level costs are seldom published; indirectness when the unit is a service or platform.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a chain of the business unit's five primary activities and four support activities, with what the unit does in each activity. It names where cost and differentiation concentrate along the chain.

technique: **Taxonomy building (classification scheme, typology, controlled vocabulary)**
what_it_does: Builds a scheme of classes and assigns items to them. Artefact: usually a hierarchy; read the spread of items across classes and items that fit no class.
fit_test: Items are often listed under several parents, many are unclassifiable, or classes cannot be told apart, which shows the chosen characteristics are wrong.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Taxonomies rely on empirical characteristics and typologies on abstract or subjective criteria. A taxonomy development technique from information systems research was not opened. ([Wikipedia, Taxonomy (general)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxonomy_(general)))
purpose: Builds a scheme of classes from observable characteristics, assigns items to the classes and produces a hierarchy and a draft codebook.
use_when: Use when you have a set of items and need a class scheme that sorts them and shows which items fit no class.
requires_minimum: A set of items with observable characteristics.
not_for_text: Items are often listed under several parents, many are unclassifiable, or classes cannot be told apart, which shows the chosen characteristics are wrong.
consumes: charter or question:agreed; raw dataset or corpus:raw
related_techniques: pairs with :: DM-06 :: Affinity grouping suggests classes from the items before the scheme is fixed; pairs with :: HE1-15 :: Content analysis applies a fixed category scheme to text and counts use
typical_model_failure: Invents classes from the item labels alone and assigns items to them without checking class overlap.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Risk of bias from the choice of characteristics; unclassified and multiply classified items lower certainty by indirectness.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a classification scheme, usually a hierarchy, with each class named and each item assigned to a class. It reports the spread of items across classes and lists the items that fit no class.

technique: **Affinity diagram (KJ method)**
what_it_does: Groups many recorded items, such as survey comments or interview quotes, into clusters that form from relationships among the items. Artefact: labelled clusters; read cluster size, number of clusters and orphan items.
fit_test: One catch-all cluster dominates, or items move between clusters when a second person sorts them.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Group membership is not set in advance; no inter-rater reliability evidence found. ([Wikipedia, Affinity diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affinity_diagram))
purpose: Groups many recorded items, such as survey comments or interview quotes, into clusters that form from the relationships among the items, and produces labelled clusters.
use_when: Use when you have many comments or quotes and want themes to emerge from the items without fixed categories.
requires_minimum: At least 20 items recorded individually.
not_for_text: One catch-all cluster dominates, or items move between clusters when a second person sorts them.
consumes: charter or question:agreed; raw dataset or corpus:raw
related_techniques: substitutes for :: MM-14 :: Hand clustering replaces document clustering when volume_class is readable by a person; pairs with :: MM-15 :: A person reads and names computer-generated groups to build themes
typical_model_failure: Forces items into clusters named after the first items seen and leaves orphan items unreported.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:human review sample; decision-informing:prompt variation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:prompt variation; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: No inter-rater reliability evidence; cluster membership is not set in advance, so reliability depends on a second sort. Risk of bias from the sorter.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a set of labelled clusters, each holding the recorded items (such as survey comments or interview quotes) that belong together. It gives the number of clusters, the size of each cluster, and the orphan items that joined no cluster.

technique: **Lens application (sorting claims by a classification lens, for example input versus outcome)**
what_it_does: Sorts a set of claims or measures by a chosen set of categories so that mixed kinds of claim can be compared by type. Artefact: a table of claims by category; many claims in one category (inputs) and few in another (outcomes) shows that evidence of a kind is missing.
fit_test: Claims cannot be assigned reliably, or two raters assign them differently, which shows the category definitions are unclear.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** No opened source describes lens application as a named technique. The nearest documented distinction is input, output, outcome and impact in logic models, which was not searched.
purpose: Sorts a set of claims or measures by chosen categories, such as input or outcome, and produces a table of claims by category.
use_when: Use when claims of different kinds are mixed and you want to compare them by type and see which kind of evidence is missing.
requires_minimum: A set of claims or indicators and written category definitions.
not_for_text: Claims cannot be assigned reliably, or two raters assign them differently, which shows the category definitions are unclear.
consumes: charter or question:agreed; raw dataset or corpus:raw
related_techniques: pairs with :: CM1-14 :: Absence analysis reads an empty category as a missing kind of evidence; pairs with :: DM-05 :: Taxonomy building supplies the categories when none exist
typical_model_failure: Assigns borderline claims to the most common category, which hides the weak categories that the technique is meant to expose.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:human review sample; decision-informing:prompt variation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:prompt variation; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Rater disagreement on category assignment lowers certainty by inconsistency; no source describes this as a named technique.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table of claims or measures sorted by the categories of the chosen lens, with each claim shown in one category. It gives the count in each category and names any category with few or no entries, which shows that evidence of that kind is missing.

technique: **Two by two matrix (quadrant analysis)** Also serves: Assess actors, options and risks; Project forward.
what_it_does: Places items on two chosen dimensions so that each is assigned to one of four cells. Artefact: items plotted or sorted into quadrants; read the count per quadrant and clusters near cell boundaries.
fit_test: Items cluster on one axis, the two dimensions are correlated, or ratings differ between raters.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** Uses of the form are documented for SWOT ([Wikipedia, SWOT analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SWOT_analysis)) and stakeholder grids ([Wikipedia, Stakeholder analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stakeholder_analysis)), but no source was found that evaluates the two by two matrix as a general technique. Scenario and stakeholder versions have their own rows.
purpose: Places items on two chosen dimensions so that each falls into one of four cells and produces a quadrant table.
use_when: Use when items can be rated on two dimensions and you want a quick sort into four groups.
requires_minimum: At least six items and a defensible scale on each dimension.
not_for_text: Items cluster on one axis, the two dimensions are correlated, or ratings differ between raters.
consumes: charter or question:agreed; raw dataset or corpus:raw
related_techniques: pairs with :: AO-02 :: The power-interest grid is a two by two matrix with fixed axes; pairs with :: PJ-13 :: A scenario matrix uses two uncertainty axes with the same quadrant logic
typical_model_failure: Rates items on each axis from general impressions, giving ratings that cannot be reproduced or defended.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:human review sample; decision-informing:prompt variation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:prompt variation; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Rater differences and the choice of dimensions lower certainty by risk of bias and inconsistency; no source evaluates the form as a general technique.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result places each item in one of four quadrants defined by the two named dimensions, as a plot or a sorted list. It gives the count per quadrant and names the items close to a cell boundary.

technique: **PESTLE (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental; the shorter PEST omits legal and environmental; outside-in thinking)**
what_it_does: Sorts external factors into fixed categories. Artefact: a categorised list; many factors in one category show concentration and empty categories show possible omissions.
fit_test: Factors fit two categories (regulation as political and legal) or none, or the list has no causal links between factors.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Traced to Aguilar (1967). Helps explain past change but is not always reliable for predicting it; no controlled study found. The CIA primer and the UK handbook use the same list under the name outside-in thinking, also without effect evidence. ([Wikipedia, PEST analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PEST_analysis); [CIA Tradecraft Primer (2009)](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Tradecraft-Primer-apr09.pdf); [UK Red Teaming Handbook](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1027158/20210625-Red_Teaming_Handbook.pdf))
purpose: Sorts external factors into political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental categories and produces a categorised list.

Outputs are often unused in later strategy stages (Hill and Westbrook 1997, cited there) and the origin is disputed. ([Wikipedia, SWOT analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SWOT_analysis))
purpose: Sorts factors into internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats and produces a two by two matrix.

not_for_text: A factor is internal or external depending on viewpoint, or the matrix fills with generic items.

technique: **Porter's Five Forces (industry structure analysis)**
what_it_does: Assesses industry attractiveness through rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Artefact: a five-force diagram with each force rated; read which forces are strong.

status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Widely used. Coyne and Subramaniam (1996) and Wernerfelt (1984) are cited there as critics; no controlled study found. ([Wikipedia, Porter's five forces analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porter%27s_five_forces_analysis))
purpose: Rates rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power and produces a five-force diagram with each force rated.
use_when: Use when you want to judge how attractive an industry is and which competitive pressures are strong.
requires_minimum: Industry-level data on concentration, switching costs, entry barriers and substitutes.
not_for_text: Complementors, government or innovation dominate outcomes, or the industry boundary is unclear.

technique: **Cynefin framework**
what_it_does: Classifies a situation, or each part of it, as clear, complicated, complex, chaotic or confusion by the relation of cause and effect, which fixes the suitable response. Artefact: a domain assignment; read the share of parts in each domain.
fit_test: People disagree about which domain a part belongs to, or the classification changes each time it is made.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Critics call it confusing and in need of a more rigorous basis; labels changed repeatedly from 1999 to 2024; the page describes no controlled testing. ([Wikipedia, Cynefin framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynefin_framework))
purpose: Classifies a situation, or each part of it, as clear, complicated, complex, chaotic or confusion by the relation of cause and effect and produces a domain assignment.
use_when: Use when you need to decide what kind of response a situation calls for and cause and effect are in question.
requires_minimum: A situation and a judgement of whether cause and effect are known, analysable, visible only afterwards, or not discernible.
not_for_text: People disagree about which domain a part belongs to, or the classification changes each time it is made.
related_techniques: pairs with :: DM-19 :: A causal loop diagram helps test whether cause and effect are knowable
typical_model_failure: Assigns a domain from the surface features of the description and states a confident classification where the causal judgement is contestable.

output_spec: The result assigns the situation, or each part of it, to one domain (clear, complicated, complex, chaotic or confusion), with the cause and effect relation that justifies the assignment and the response that domain suits. It gives the share of parts in each domain.

not_for_text: Behaviour matches two archetypes equally or none. The label should follow the loop structure and not replace it.

technique: **Leverage points (Meadows' twelve places to intervene in a system)**
what_it_does: Ranks types of intervention in a system from least to most effective, from constants and parameters (twelfth) to the power to transcend paradigms (first). Artefact: an ordered list; read the level at which a proposed intervention acts.
fit_test: An intervention fits several levels, or its real effect contradicts the ranking. Meadows says exceptions to every item can change its rank.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Meadows calls the list tentative and its order unreliable in places; no empirical test of the ranking was found. ([Donella Meadows Project, Leverage points](https://donellameadows.org/archives/leverage-points-places-to-intervene-in-a-system/))
purpose: Ranks types of intervention in a system from least to most effective and produces an ordered list showing the level at which a proposed intervention acts.
use_when: Use when you want to judge whether a proposed intervention in a system acts at a weak or a strong level.
requires_minimum: A described system with its feedback structure, rules, information flows and goals.
not_for_text: An intervention fits several levels, or its real effect contradicts the ranking. Meadows says exceptions to every item can change its rank.

related_techniques: should follow :: DM-19 :: The feedback structure of the system must be known before intervention levels can be assigned; pairs with :: DM-13 :: An archetype names the structure that the intervention targets
typical_model_failure: Places an intervention at a level by its name and treats the published order as a fixed ranking.

error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Meadows calls the list tentative and its order unreliable in places; no empirical test of the ranking was found.

output_spec: The result is an ordered list of intervention types from the twelfth (constants and parameters) to the first (the power to transcend paradigms), with the proposed intervention placed on it. It states the level at which the proposed intervention acts.

technique: **Wardley mapping**
what_it_does: Positions the components of a service by visibility to the user and by evolution stage (genesis, custom build, product, commodity), with dependency lines. Artefact: a two-axis map; read components placed at the wrong stage for how they are treated.
fit_test: Placement on the evolution axis cannot be agreed or evidenced, so the map records opinion only.
status_and_evidence: **Practice.** The source page has notices about self-published sources and unsupported statements; critics say it can turn assumptions into apparent facts; no independent evaluation found. ([Wikipedia, Wardley map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardley_map))
purpose: Positions the components of a service by visibility to the user and by evolution stage, with dependency lines, and produces a two-axis map.
use_when: Use when you want to see which components of a service are treated as if they were at a different stage of maturity than they are.
requires_minimum: A defined user and need, the components that meet it, and a judgement of each evolution stage.
not_for_text: Placement on the evolution axis cannot be agreed or evidenced, so the map records opinion only.

Each component of the service is placed on the map with dependency lines between components, and the components placed at the wrong stage for how they are treated are named.

technique: **Levels-of-analysis models (Marr's three levels, micro, meso and macro levels)**
what_it_does: Examines the topic at several distinct levels, each answering a different kind of question. Artefact: findings organised by level; read levels with no findings and contradictions between levels.
fit_test: Levels interact so strongly that findings cannot be assigned to one, or an important effect lies between levels.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Levels are not necessarily exclusive, and the framework is widely discussed but rarely applied in scholarly articles in international relations. Marr (1982) was not opened. ([Wikipedia, Marr's levels of analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marr%27s_levels_of_analysis))
purpose: Examines a topic at several distinct levels, each answering a different kind of question, and produces findings organised by level.
use_when: Use when a question can be answered at more than one level, such as individual, organisation and system, and you need to know which levels have findings.
requires_minimum: The topic and a chosen set of levels.
not_for_text: Levels interact so strongly that findings cannot be assigned to one, or an important effect lies between levels.
related_techniques: pairs with :: FQ-04 :: Reframing also changes the level of analysis; pairs with :: FQ-05 :: Multiple models can be chosen to match the levels
typical_model_failure: Assigns findings to a level by keyword, leaving the empty levels unreported.

error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: Levels are not necessarily exclusive and the framework is rarely applied in scholarly articles in some fields; cross-level contradictions lower certainty by inconsistency.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result has findings organised under each level examined (such as micro, meso and macro, or the three levels of Marr), with the kind of question each level answers stated. It names the levels with no findings and lists the contradictions between levels.

technique: **Design structure matrix (dependency structure matrix)**
what_it_does: Records which element depends on or supplies which in a square matrix, then reorders it to reveal clusters or sequence. Artefact: a reordered matrix; read clusters, coupled blocks and the elements affected by a change.
fit_test: Reordering never produces clusters or a stable order, which suggests the elements are defined at the wrong granularity.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Origin traced to Steward in the 1960s; minimising feedback works for binary matrices but not always for numeric ones. ([Wikipedia, Design structure matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_structure_matrix))

use_when: Use when a system has many interdependent parts and you need to see clusters, coupled blocks or the parts affected by a change.
requires_minimum: At least 8 elements and the directed links between them.
not_for_text: Reordering never produces clusters or a stable order, which suggests the elements are defined at the wrong granularity.

related_techniques: pairs with :: DM-17 :: A flow diagram gives the sequence that the matrix reorders
typical_model_failure: Reorders the matrix by hand or by reading and mislabels dependencies, instead of running a reordering algorithm in code.

error_sources: input data; data transformation; statistical assumptions
certainty_limits: Minimising feedback works for binary matrices but not always for numeric ones; the result depends on how elements are defined and on the reordering method.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a square matrix of the elements recording which depends on or supplies which, reordered so that clusters or sequence show. It names the clusters, the coupled blocks, and the elements affected by a change.

technique: **Causal loop diagram** Also serves: Trace cause and test claims.
what_it_does: Draws variables and signed causal links so that reinforcing and balancing loops and delays can be identified. Artefact: a diagram with loop labels; read which loops dominate and where delays could cause oscillation.
fit_test: No feedback loop can be drawn or links cannot be given a defensible polarity; a tree or a linear chain may suit the topic better.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** The source page reports no empirical evaluation. ([Wikipedia, Causal loop diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causal_loop_diagram))
purpose: Draws variables and signed causal links so that reinforcing and balancing loops and delays can be identified, and produces a diagram with loop labels.
use_when: Use when you suspect feedback between factors and want to see which loops dominate and where delays could cause oscillation.
requires_minimum: A list of variables, the judged direction and polarity of each link, and known delays.
not_for_text: No feedback loop can be drawn or links cannot be given a defensible polarity, in which case a tree or a linear chain may suit the topic better.

related_techniques: pairs with :: DM-20 :: Stock and flow modelling turns the loops into quantities that can be simulated; pairs with :: DM-13 :: Archetypes name recurring loop structures

certainty_limits: Link polarity is a judgement and the source reports no empirical evaluation, so the diagram is a hypothesis about structure; risk of bias and imprecision on delays.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a diagram of variables joined by signed causal links, with each reinforcing or balancing loop labelled and delays marked. It names the loops that dominate and the places where delays could cause oscillation.

technique: **Stock and flow modelling (system dynamics, including simulation)** Also serves: Project forward.
what_it_does: Represents accumulations that change only through inflows and outflows, and when simulated produces time paths. Artefact: a diagram and simulated paths; read accumulation, durations and sensitivity to parameters, not point values.

Simulation accuracy is contested: a 2008 working paper by Turner reportedly found that observed data tracked the Limits to Growth standard run, but it was not opened.

use_when: Use when the question concerns a quantity that builds up or runs down over time and you want to see durations and sensitivity to assumptions.
requires_minimum: Stocks, flows, units and initial values, plus calibration data and parameters for simulation.
not_for_text: The quantity cannot be framed as an accumulation, flow data are unavailable, the model cannot reproduce the history it should explain, or the conclusion rests on one untested parameter.

related_techniques: should follow :: DM-19 :: A causal loop diagram identifies the feedback that the stock and flow structure must include; pairs with :: TC1-17 :: Sensitivity analysis tests which parameters drive the paths

output_spec: The result is a diagram of stocks, inflows and outflows with the simulated time path of each stock. It reports accumulation, durations and sensitivity to parameters, and does not rest on point values.

subgroup: Compare with another case, period or position
technique: **Historical analogy and parallel analysis (likenesses and differences, analogical explanation)**
what_it_does: Places the present topic beside one or more past cases and lists where they resemble and differ. Artefact: a likenesses and differences table with each element rated (strong, moderate, weak, not analogous); correspondence supports applying a lesson to the present case and divergence marks where it must not be applied.
fit_test: The listed differences are never checked against the mechanism that produced the earlier outcome, only one analogy is tested, or a vivid case is chosen because it is memorable.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described in method texts and in studies of misuse (vividness bias; Bundy's use of Dien Bien Phu for Vietnam in 1965 fitted poorly). No study comparing analogy with other techniques on accuracy was found. ([Neustadt and May, Thinking in Time (summary)](https://obsidianrook.com/doomfiles/THINKING_IN_TIME.html); [CIA, Analogical Reasoning in Intelligence Analysis](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/6-Analogical_Reasoning_in_Intelligence_Analysis.pdf); [Khong, Analogies at War (Project MUSE record)](https://muse.jhu.edu/book/74147))
purpose: Places the present topic beside a past case and rates each likeness and difference, producing a likenesses and differences table that shows where a lesson from the past case may and may not be applied.
use_when: Use when a user asks whether a past episode is a fair guide to the present one, or what a similar earlier case suggests will happen.
requires_minimum: At least one past case with established facts, timeline and outcome, and a statement of what is known, unclear and presumed about the present case.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when only one analogy is tested, when the case was picked because it is memorable, or when the listed differences are never checked against the mechanism that produced the earlier outcome.
consumes: charter or question:agreed; raw dataset or corpus:raw
related_techniques: should follow :: CM1-06 :: choosing the past case by a stated rule reduces the pull of a vivid case; pairs with :: PJ-02 :: a base rate from many similar cases corrects reliance on a single analogy; pairs with :: TC1-04 :: process tracing tests whether the earlier mechanism operated in the present case
typical_model_failure: Picks the most famous past case, lists likenesses at length and leaves out differences in the mechanism that produced the earlier outcome.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; decision-informing:source-span citation; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:source-span citation; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:expert review
error_sources: input data; source selection; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when only one analogy is used, when the case was chosen for vividness (risk of bias), or when the earlier mechanism is not shown to apply now (indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table of likenesses and differences between the present topic and each past case, with each element rated strong, moderate, weak or not analogous. It names the elements where the cases correspond, which support applying a lesson to the present case, and the elements where they diverge, where the lesson must not be applied.

subgroup: Compare with another case, period or position
technique: **Mill's method of agreement and most different systems design (MDSD)**
what_it_does: Looks for the factor present in every case that shows the outcome, across dissimilar contexts. Artefact: a table of candidate factors by case; the factor common to all is the candidate cause.

subgroup: Compare over time, against peers, forecasters or a standard
technique: **Gap analysis**
what_it_does: Compares current with desired performance. Artefact: a prioritised list of gaps and the means to close each; read the largest or most critical gaps.
fit_test: No clear target state exists, or the benchmark is unsuitable.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** The source page notes the term is used inconsistently. ([Wikipedia, Gap analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gap_analysis))
purpose: Compares current with desired performance, producing a prioritised list of gaps and the means to close each.
use_when: Use when a user asks how far a current state is from a target and what to do first to close the distance.
requires_minimum: A description of current resources and capabilities, a target or benchmark, and the requirements to meet.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when no clear target state exists or the benchmark is unsuitable. The term is used inconsistently, so confirm the definition with the user.

related_techniques: should follow :: CM1-12 :: benchmarking supplies an external target state; pairs with :: AO-12 :: weighted criteria make the priority order of gaps explicit

output_spec: The result is a prioritised list of gaps, each row naming the current performance, the desired performance, the size of the gap and the means to close it. The largest or most critical gaps come first, and the result ends by naming them.

subgroup: Compare over time, against peers, forecasters or a standard
technique: **Maturity model and capability assessment (Capability Maturity Model Integration, CMMI)**
what_it_does: Rates processes against staged levels to show where an organisation stands and what to improve. Artefact: a maturity level or capability profile.
fit_test: Processes are not repeatable or not comparable to the reference model, or the organisation is small or agile.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** The model says what processes should exist, not how to implement them, and results do not guarantee gains in every organisation. Generic non-software frameworks were not researched. ([Wikipedia, Capability Maturity Model Integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capability_Maturity_Model_Integration))
purpose: Rates processes against staged levels, producing a maturity level or capability profile that shows where an organisation stands and what to improve.
use_when: Use when a user asks how mature an organisation processes are against a reference model, or what the next level would require.
requires_minimum: Evidence on each process named in the reference model, normally documents and interviews in a formal appraisal. Public evidence supports only a provisional rating.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when processes are not repeatable or not comparable to the reference model, or when the organisation is small or works in an agile way. The model says what processes should exist, not how to implement them.

related_techniques: pairs with :: CM1-15 :: the gap to the next level can be listed and prioritised; should follow :: HE1-18 :: documents are read systematically for stated practice before a level is assigned
typical_model_failure: Assigns a level from policy statements and marketing about processes instead of evidence of practice, and applies a software model to a non-software process.

output_spec: The result is a table of processes with the staged level assigned to each and the reason for that level, followed by a maturity level or capability profile for the organisation as a whole. It names the processes to improve first.

technique: Sponsor versus non-sponsor comparison (meta-epidemiological sponsorship analysis)
what_it_does: Compares the share of favourable results and conclusions between sponsored and independently funded reports on one topic. Artefact: a risk ratio or odds ratio. In health research the risk ratios were 1.27 for favourable efficacy results and 1.34 for favourable conclusions.
fit_test: Needs enough independent reports on one question. The health studies are observational, so the result is an association. The harms result was not significant. No study of surveys or consultancy reports was found, so applying the result to them is an inference.
status_and_evidence: Documented. A Cochrane review of 75 papers found the pattern was not explained by standard risk of bias items. An older review of 30 studies gave an odds ratio of 4.05. ([Lundh et al. 2017, Cochrane abstract](https://cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.MR000033.pub3/pdf/CDSR/MR000033/MR000033_abstract.pdf); [Cochrane summary page, industry sponsorship and research outcome](https://www.cochrane.org/MR000033/METHOD_industry-sponsorship-and-research-outcome); [Pharmaceutical industry sponsorship and research outcome and quality](https://escholarship.org/content/qt8g62x69s/qt8g62x69s.pdf?t=lnr10g))
purpose: Compares the share of favourable results and conclusions between sponsored and independently funded reports on one topic, producing a risk ratio or odds ratio.
use_when: Use when a user asks whether industry or sponsor funding is linked to more favourable findings in the reports on a topic.
requires_minimum: Enough independent and sponsored reports on one question to form a ratio, with a funder recorded for each report.
not_for_text: Needs enough independent reports on one question. Health studies are observational, so the result is an association. No study of surveys or consultancy reports was found, so applying the health result to them is an inference.
consumes: charter or question:agreed; raw dataset or corpus:raw
related_techniques: pairs with :: HE1-02 :: a per-source quality rating covers accuracy, which a funding comparison does not; should follow :: HE1-08 :: a systematic search supplies a defensible set of reports to compare
typical_model_failure: Assigns a sponsor from the logo alone and treats independence as proof of quality.

error_sources: input data; source selection; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Certainty drops because the evidence is observational (risk of bias), when few reports fall in one group (imprecision), and when the result is carried from health studies to other fields (indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result gives the number of sponsored and independently funded reports on the topic and the share of favourable results and favourable conclusions in each group. It reports a risk ratio or odds ratio for each of results and conclusions, and ends with a statement of what the ratio shows about sponsorship.

technique: **Five whys**
what_it_does: Asks 'why' repeatedly about a problem to reach a cause treated as the root. Artefact: one chain of causes; read the final cause.
fit_test: Different teams reach different answers, or the chain ends where the questioning happened to stop. It follows a single causal path.
status_and_evidence: **Practice.** A peer-reviewed commentary finds no evidence of effectiveness, recommends against its use for root cause analysis in patient safety, and reports a worked example with 30 causal pathways of which the technique would address one or two. Figures were read through a summarising tool and need checking. ([BMJ Quality and Safety 2017;26:671, on the five whys](https://qualitysafety.bmj.com/content/26/8/671))
purpose: Asks why repeatedly about one stated problem and records a single chain of causes, leaving a candidate root cause as a result.
use_when: Use when you need a quick first account of why a problem happened and one plausible causal path is enough to start an investigation.
requires_minimum: One defined problem statement and at least one person or record able to answer each why.
not_for_rules: stakes_tier=high-stakes & insight_wanted=cause :: a single causal path is not adequate for a high-stakes causal finding
not_for_text: Wrong choice when different teams reach different answers or the chain ends where the questioning happened to stop. Misused when the final answer is called the root cause without checking other causal paths.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-02 :: the fishbone diagram shows the many causal paths that one why chain leaves out; pairs with :: TC1-03 :: a fault tree tests whether combinations of events, not one chain, cause the problem
typical_model_failure: Produces a tidy chain of five answers that stops at a plausible but untested cause and presents it as the root cause.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:expert review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; expert opinion
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when answers rest on opinion and not on records, when the chain follows one of several causal paths, or when different people reach different chains (inconsistency and indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is one chain of causes, written in order from the stated problem to the final cause, with each link answering why the one before it occurred. It ends by naming the final cause as the root cause.

technique: **Fishbone diagram (Ishikawa diagram, cause and effect diagram)**
what_it_does: Groups brainstormed causes of one problem under category branches. Artefact: a diagram with the problem as head and categories as ribs; read categories holding many causes and empty categories.
fit_test: Many causes fit two categories, a large 'other' rib appears, or problems, causes and symptoms are confused.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** One of the seven basic tools of quality control; application claims on the page have 'citation needed' tags; the BMJ commentary lists it among alternatives to five whys without effect evidence. ([Wikipedia, Ishikawa diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishikawa_diagram); [BMJ Quality and Safety 2017;26:671, on the five whys](https://qualitysafety.bmj.com/content/26/8/671))
purpose: Groups brainstormed causes of one problem under category branches and produces a fishbone diagram with the problem as its head.
use_when: Use when a team needs to list and sort the many possible causes of one problem before deciding which to investigate.
requires_minimum: A defined problem, a list of causes (brainstormed or taken from documents) and a category scheme chosen before grouping.
not_for_rules: stakes_tier=high-stakes & insight_wanted=cause :: the diagram lists proposed causes and does not test any of them
not_for_text: Wrong choice when many causes fit two categories, a large other branch appears, or problems, causes and symptoms are confused. Misused when the number of causes on a branch is read as its importance.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-01 :: a why chain follows one branch of the diagram in depth; should follow :: family:Frame the question :: the problem must be stated before causes are grouped
typical_model_failure: Fills every category with generic causes that were not raised by anyone and treats the count of causes on a branch as evidence of importance.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; expert opinion
certainty_limits: Certainty is low because the diagram records proposed causes and not tested ones. It falls further when all causes come from one brainstorming group.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a diagram with the problem as the head and category branches as ribs, with the brainstormed causes listed under the category each belongs to. It names the categories holding many causes and the categories left empty.

technique: **Fault tree analysis** Also serves: Assess actors, options and risks.
what_it_does: Starts from one undesired top event and works downward through AND and OR gates to the combinations of lower events that cause it. Artefact: a gate tree with minimal cut sets; read short cut sets and single points of failure.
fit_test: Important failures cannot be placed in the tree, or the top event is too broad for one tree. It is weaker than failure mode and effects analysis for listing all initiating faults.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described, with standards named on the page. ([Wikipedia, Fault tree analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_tree_analysis))
purpose: Works downward from one undesired top event through AND and OR gates to produce a gate tree with minimal cut sets.
use_when: Use when one specific failure or bad outcome must be traced to the combinations of lower events that could cause it.
requires_minimum: One precisely defined top event and system knowledge of the lower events. Failure rates are needed only to compute probabilities.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when important failures cannot be placed in the tree or the top event is too broad for one tree. It is weaker than failure mode and effects analysis for listing all initiating faults.
related_techniques: pairs with :: AO-16 :: failure mode and effects analysis lists initiating faults that a tree built from the top event can miss; pairs with :: AO-17 :: a bow-tie adds barriers and consequences to the same causal paths
typical_model_failure: Leaves out common-cause failures and treats listed events as independent when multiplying their probabilities.
