error_sources: input data; statistical assumptions; expert opinion
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when failure data are missing or taken from other systems, when events are not independent, or when the top event is too broad (indirectness and imprecision).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a gate tree that starts from one top event and shows the AND and OR gates down to the lower events. It lists the minimal cut sets, and it names the short cut sets and any single points of failure.

technique: **Process tracing (diagnostic tests: straw in the wind, hoop, smoking gun, doubly decisive)**
what_it_does: Examines diagnostic evidence within one case and compares what each rival hypothesis predicts with what is found. Artefact: a test result per hypothesis; failing a hoop test eliminates a hypothesis and passing a smoking gun test supports it strongly.
fit_test: The evidence is not diagnostic given prior knowledge, or the rival set is incomplete. It is often unclear which test applies, and doubly decisive tests are rarely achieved in social science.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** A critic disputes how the tests map to necessity and sufficiency. The Magenta Book suggests it for single cases with no counterfactual. ([Collier, Understanding Process Tracing](https://polisci.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/people/u3827/Understanding%20Process%20Tracing.pdf); [BetterEvaluation commentary on process tracing tests](https://www.mande.co.uk/2015/uncategorized/straws-in-the-wind-hoops-and-smoking-guns-what-can-process-tracing-offer-to-impact-evaluation/); [Magenta Book, Annex A, analytical methods for use within an evaluation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/magenta-book-annex-a-analytical-methods-for-use-within-an-evaluation-html))
purpose: Tests what each rival hypothesis predicts against diagnostic evidence within one case and produces a test result per hypothesis in a hypotheses matrix.
use_when: Use when you need to decide which of several explanations fits the detailed evidence in a single case and no comparison group exists.
requires_minimum: Detailed evidence from one case and at least two rival hypotheses, each with predictions written before the evidence is read.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the evidence is not diagnostic given prior knowledge or the rival set is incomplete. It is often unclear which test applies, and doubly decisive tests are rare in social science.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-13 :: analysis of competing hypotheses compares all evidence across all hypotheses while process tracing sets the strength of each test; pairs with :: CM1-05 :: comparative cases show whether the traced mechanism recurs
typical_model_failure: Classifies a piece of evidence as a smoking gun after seeing it and not before, and ignores rival hypotheses that were never stated.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; decision-informing:source-span citation; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:source-span citation; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; source selection; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when the rival set is incomplete, when test strength is judged after the evidence is seen, or when the documents come from interested parties (risk of bias).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table of diagnostic evidence items against each rival hypothesis, giving the test type (straw in the wind, hoop, smoking gun) and the outcome of the test for each hypothesis. It names the hypotheses eliminated by a failed hoop test and the hypotheses strongly supported by a passed smoking gun test.

technique: **Counterfactual analysis (potential outcomes, minimal rewrite of history)** Also serves: Compare.
what_it_does: Sets the actual outcome against an argued account of what would have happened had one factor differed. Artefact: a counterfactual scenario; read divergence from the actual outcome as the causal effect of the factor.
fit_test: Varying the factor requires changing other factors that would also matter (low cotenability). Fewer required changes make the inference easier to defend; a 'but for' condition is not automatically a cause.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Fearon argues counterfactuals are unavoidable in causal testing with few cases; the Stanford Encyclopedia lists vagueness of similarity and counterfactual scepticism as limits. ([Fearon, Counterfactuals and Hypothesis Testing in Political Science](https://web.stanford.edu/group/fearon-research/cgi-bin/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2013/10/Counterfactuals-and-Hypothesis-Testing-in-Political-Science.pdf); [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Counterfactuals](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/counterfactuals/))
purpose: Sets the actual outcome against an argued account of what would have happened had one factor differed and produces a counterfactual scenario.
use_when: Use when you must judge whether one factor caused an outcome in a single case and no comparison data exist.
requires_minimum: One specified change to a single factor, the relevant historical facts, and a stated theory or regularity linking the factor to the outcome.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when varying the factor requires changing other factors that would also matter (low cotenability). A but-for condition is not automatically a cause.
related_techniques: substitutes for :: TC1-06 :: when no comparison group or before and after data exist (access_depth=narrative only); pairs with :: TC1-04 :: process tracing supplies the within-case evidence the counterfactual is checked against
typical_model_failure: Rewrites history so that several other factors change at once, then credits the divergence to the one factor named.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; expert opinion
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when the change needs other changes, when the theory linking factor to outcome is weak, or when the argued outcome cannot be checked against any evidence (indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result states the actual outcome, the one factor that is changed, and a counterfactual scenario describing what would have happened had that factor differed. It ends with the divergence between the scenario and the actual outcome, read as the causal effect of the factor.

technique: **Difference-in-differences** Also serves: Compare.
what_it_does: Compares the change over time in a treated group with the change over time in a control group. Artefact: the interaction coefficient (treatment group by post period), read as the treatment effect.
fit_test: The groups would not have changed by the same amount without treatment (parallel trends fails), a concurrent shock affected one group, or group composition changed.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described on an encyclopaedia page. ([Wikipedia, Difference in differences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Difference_in_differences))
purpose: Compares the change over time in a treated group with the change in a control group and produces an interaction coefficient read as the treatment effect.
use_when: Use when a policy or event affected one group and not another and you want to know how much it changed an outcome.
time_structure: requires=panel; requires=repeated cross-section; requires=aggregate time series
requires_minimum: At least one treated and one comparison group, with at least one period before and one after treatment. Several pre-treatment periods are needed to check parallel trends.
not_for_rules: time_structure=cross-section :: the design needs observations before and after treatment
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the groups would not have changed by the same amount without treatment (parallel trends fails), a concurrent shock affected one group, or group composition changed.
related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-08 :: the graph shows which covariates to include and which to leave out; pairs with :: TC1-17 :: varying pre-periods, controls and group definitions tests the parallel trends assumption; substitutes for :: CM1-11 :: when a comparison group exists and time_structure=panel|repeated cross-section|aggregate time series
typical_model_failure: Runs the interaction regression without checking pre-treatment trends, reads the coefficient as causal, and reports standard errors that ignore clustering.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; decision-informing:sensitivity analysis; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:sensitivity analysis; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:expert review
error_sources: input data; statistical assumptions; data transformation
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when pre-treatment trends differ, a concurrent shock hit one group, group composition changed, or there are few clusters or periods (risk of bias and imprecision).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result gives the outcome for the treated and control groups before and after the change, and the change over time in each group. It ends with the interaction coefficient (treatment group by post period) and states it as the treatment effect.

technique: **Quasi-experimental designs (natural experiment, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity)**
what_it_does: Each uses existing data in which exposure is assigned as if at random: by an event or rule (natural experiment), by a variable that changes exposure but affects the outcome only through it (instrument), or by a cutoff (discontinuity). Artefact: an effect estimate under stated assumptions.
fit_test: Assignment is related to outcomes, the instrument is weak or has a direct effect, or units can manipulate their position relative to the cutoff.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** The Hernán and Robins book lists instrumental variables among its topics, but the assumptions here come from general knowledge and no source on natural experiments or regression discontinuity was opened. ([Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook))
purpose: Estimates an effect from observational data in which exposure was assigned as if at random (natural experiment, instrument or cutoff) and produces an effect estimate under stated assumptions.
use_when: Use when a randomised trial is impossible but an event, rule, instrument or threshold gave some units exposure for reasons unrelated to the outcome.
requires_minimum: Record-level data with exposure and outcome, plus a clear assignment event, a valid instrument or a running variable with a cutoff. Discontinuity designs need enough records near the cutoff.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when assignment is related to outcomes, the instrument is weak or affects the outcome directly, or units can manipulate their position relative to the cutoff.
related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-08 :: the graph states which paths the instrument or cutoff must not open; substitutes for :: TC1-06 :: when no untreated comparison group with pre-treatment data exists (time_structure=cross-section) but an instrument or cutoff does; pairs with :: TC1-17 :: sensitivity checks vary the bandwidth, instrument and controls
typical_model_failure: Accepts an instrument or cutoff without testing its assumptions and reports a precise estimate that depends on an invalid design.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; decision-informing:sensitivity analysis; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:sensitivity analysis; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:expert review
error_sources: input data; statistical assumptions; data transformation
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when the instrument is weak or has a direct effect, when units manipulate the cutoff, or when the estimate applies only to a narrow group of units (risk of bias and indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result names the design used (natural experiment, instrument or discontinuity) and describes the event, rule, variable or cutoff that assigns exposure as if at random. It gives an effect estimate and lists the assumptions under which the estimate holds.

technique: **Confounder identification with directed acyclic graphs (adjustment sets, backdoor criterion)**
what_it_does: Draws assumed causal links to decide which variables to adjust for and which to leave alone. Artefact: a diagram and an adjustment set.
fit_test: Important common causes are unmeasured, or a collider or mediator is adjusted for, which can add bias.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** The book lists the topic, but detailed assumptions were not read. ([Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook))
purpose: Draws assumed causal links as a directed acyclic graph and produces a diagram and an adjustment set of variables to include and to leave out.
use_when: Use when you must decide which variables to control for before estimating an effect and the causal links can be defended from subject knowledge.
requires_minimum: A named exposure and outcome, and subject knowledge strong enough to defend each assumed link.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when important common causes are unmeasured, or when a collider or mediator is adjusted for, which can add bias. The graph encodes assumptions and does not estimate anything by itself.
related_techniques: pairs with :: DM-19 :: a causal loop diagram shows feedback that an acyclic graph cannot represent; pairs with :: TC1-07 :: the chosen adjustment set feeds the estimate
typical_model_failure: Draws links to match the data at hand and not prior knowledge, or includes a collider or mediator in the adjustment set.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; expert opinion; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when links are untested, when relevant common causes are unmeasured, or when experts disagree on the graph (risk of bias). The ceiling is estimate an intervention effect because the graph states what must be adjusted for, and the estimate comes from another technique.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result has a diagram of the assumed causal links between the variables and an adjustment set naming the variables to adjust for and the variables to leave alone. It also has a register of the causal assumptions the diagram depends on.

technique: **Logic model and theory of change**
what_it_does: Maps the expected causal chain from inputs to outcomes with the assumptions behind each step. Artefact: a diagram or narrative of if-then links; read the weakest assumption and the strength of evidence at each link.
fit_test: Outcomes may result from processes outside the program so that success is wrongly credited to it. Models vary widely in components.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** The Magenta Book defines a theory of change as a synthesis of existing evidence; the logic model page gives inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes. ([Magenta Book, central government guidance on evaluation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/magenta-book-central-government-guidance-on-evaluation-html); [Wikipedia, Logic model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_model))
purpose: Maps the expected causal chain from inputs to outcomes with the assumption behind each step and produces a logic model or theory of change.
use_when: Use when you need to set out how a program is meant to produce its outcomes and where its weakest assumptions are.
requires_minimum: Program documents or accounts that state inputs, activities and intended outcomes.

technique: **Contribution analysis**
what_it_does: Builds a reasoned line of evidence that a program contributed to an outcome when an experiment is not possible. Artefact: an evidenced contribution story; it is not definitive proof.
fit_test: The theory of change is poor, because the quality of the analysis depends on it. No precise effect size results.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described in government evaluation guidance. ([Magenta Book, Annex A, analytical methods for use within an evaluation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/magenta-book-annex-a-analytical-methods-for-use-within-an-evaluation-html))

use_when: Use when you must judge whether a program helped cause an outcome and an experiment or comparison group is not possible.
requires_minimum: A stated theory of change, evidence for each link, and a list of other influences on the outcome.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the theory of change is poor, because the quality of the analysis depends on it. No precise effect size results, and the story is not proof.
related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-09 :: the theory of change and its assumptions supply the links to be tested; substitutes for :: TC1-06 :: when no comparison group or outcome tables exist (access_depth=narrative only)

technique: **Realist evaluation (context, mechanism, outcome configurations)**
what_it_does: Tests what works, for whom and in what circumstances. Artefact: a refined program theory; suited to new or scaled programs and programs with mixed outcomes.
fit_test: Only the average net effect is needed, outcome data are unavailable, the program is simple, or resources are lacking. It is time consuming and mechanisms are inferred.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described in government guidance. ([Magenta Book, realist evaluation supplementary guide](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/supplementary-guide-realist-evaluation-html); [Magenta Book, Annex A, analytical methods for use within an evaluation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/magenta-book-annex-a-analytical-methods-for-use-within-an-evaluation-html))
purpose: Tests what works for whom and in what circumstances through context, mechanism and outcome configurations and produces a refined program theory.
use_when: Use when average results hide differences and you need to know why a program works in some settings and not others.
requires_minimum: Evaluation questions, hypotheses stated as context, mechanism and outcome configurations, and outcome data for different groups or settings.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when only the average net effect is needed, outcome data are unavailable, the program is simple, or time and resources are short. It is time consuming and mechanisms are inferred.

related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-09 :: the program theory supplies the initial configurations to test; pairs with :: TC1-12 :: an impact estimate gives the average effect that realist evaluation then explains
typical_model_failure: Labels factors as mechanisms without evidence that they operate, and reports configurations that fit the data by construction.

technique: **Process evaluation and impact evaluation**
what_it_does: Process evaluation examines how an intervention was delivered; impact evaluation estimates what difference it made. Artefact: findings on delivery quality, or an attributed effect estimate; read process findings to decide whether a shortfall comes from design or delivery.
fit_test: A randomised controlled trial lacks sample size or feasible randomisation, or the control group is affected. Size of impact rarely explains why it occurred.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described in government guidance; none gives precise effect sizes from theory-based techniques. ([Magenta Book, central government guidance on evaluation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/magenta-book-central-government-guidance-on-evaluation-html); [Magenta Book, Annex A, analytical methods for use within an evaluation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/magenta-book-annex-a-analytical-methods-for-use-within-an-evaluation-html))

use_when: Use when you must separate whether a program was delivered as designed from whether it changed outcomes.
requires_minimum: Delivery data for a process evaluation. For an impact evaluation, outcome data for treated and comparison units under an experimental, quasi-experimental or theory-based design.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when a randomised trial lacks sample size or feasible randomisation, or when the control group is affected. The size of an impact rarely explains why it occurred. This record joins two designs and the impact half needs one of the estimation techniques.

related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-09 :: the logic model names the delivery steps and outcomes to examine; pairs with :: TC1-06 :: a quasi-experimental estimate supplies the impact half when no trial was run
typical_model_failure: Reports an impact estimate from a design with no valid comparison group, or reads a delivery shortfall as a design failure.

technique: **Analysis of competing hypotheses (ACH)**
what_it_does: Lists all plausible hypotheses and rates each evidence item against each, aiming to disprove hypotheses. Artefact: a hypothesis by evidence matrix; read the evidence that discriminates between hypotheses and the hypothesis with the fewest inconsistencies.
fit_test: The hypothesis list is incomplete, analysts skip steps, or non-diagnostic evidence shifts the result.
status_and_evidence: **Tested.** Tested in experiments with no accuracy benefit and some signs of harm to coherence; see the evidence section. Heuer concedes it will not always yield the right answer. ([Dhami, Belton and Mandel (2019), Strathprints record](https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/69049/); [Karvetski and Mandel (2020), Cambridge Core, does ACH help coherence](https://cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/9ED40E4658EE77914D2C7A265154B59A/S1930297500008159a.pdf/coherence-of-probability-judgments-from-uncertain-evidence-does-ach-help.pdf); [Cambridge Core paper on what works and what fails in improving analysts' accuracy](https://cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/1530E9DAE8F42B2E8FC2B5FE374DB50F/S1930297500006628a.pdf/boosting-intelligence-analysts-judgment-accuracy-what-works-what-fails.pdf); [Heuer, Psychology of Intelligence Analysis](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Pyschology-of-Intelligence-Analysis.pdf))
purpose: Lists plausible hypotheses, rates each evidence item against each, and produces a hypothesis by evidence matrix aimed at disproving hypotheses.
use_when: Use when several explanations are plausible and you need to see which evidence actually discriminates between them.
requires_minimum: At least two rival hypotheses and several evidence items rated against each.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the hypothesis list is incomplete, analysts skip steps, or non-diagnostic evidence shifts the result. Experiments found no accuracy benefit and some harm to coherence.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-16 :: a disconfirmation search tests the hypothesis that survives the matrix; substitutes for :: TC1-15 :: when evidence is available only as narrative and probabilities cannot be stated (access_depth=narrative only); pairs with :: CH-01 :: a key assumptions check exposes premises shared by every hypothesis
typical_model_failure: Rates most evidence items as consistent with every hypothesis so that nothing discriminates, and omits the hypothesis the analyst finds unlikely.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; decision-informing:source-span citation; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:source-span citation; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; source selection; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when the hypothesis list is incomplete, when evidence is not diagnostic, or when all ratings come from one analyst (risk of bias and inconsistency).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result lists the hypotheses and gives a matrix of evidence items against hypotheses with a consistency rating in each cell. It names the evidence items that discriminate between hypotheses and the hypothesis with the fewest inconsistencies.

technique: **Coherence correction and averaging of probability judgements**
what_it_does: Adjusts each analyst's probability judgements so that those on mutually exclusive hypotheses sum to one, and averages across analysts. Artefact: a corrected, aggregated judgement.
fit_test: Judgements are not on mutually exclusive, exhaustive hypotheses, or the judges share the same bias.
status_and_evidence: **Tested.** Reported to cut error by about 35 per cent (coherence correction) and about 61 per cent (averaging all 50 corrected judgements) in one laboratory task. Small homogeneous sample; attribution of the paper is unresolved. ([Cambridge Core paper on what works and what fails in improving analysts' accuracy](https://cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/1530E9DAE8F42B2E8FC2B5FE374DB50F/S1930297500006628a.pdf/boosting-intelligence-analysts-judgment-accuracy-what-works-what-fails.pdf))
purpose: Adjusts each analyst's probabilities on mutually exclusive hypotheses so they sum to one, averages across analysts, and produces a corrected aggregated judgement.
use_when: Use when several analysts have given probability estimates on the same set of hypotheses and you want one combined, internally consistent judgement.
requires_minimum: Probability judgements from at least two analysts on the same mutually exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses. More analysts improve the average.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when judgements are not on mutually exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses, or when the judges share the same bias.
related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-13 :: the matrix supplies the hypotheses on which judgements are collected; pairs with :: TC1-15 :: Bayesian updating gives coherent probabilities from a single analyst
typical_model_failure: Averages judgements that share one source or bias, or normalises probabilities over a hypothesis set that is not exhaustive.

It ends with a corrected, aggregated probability for each hypothesis, averaged across analysts.

technique: **Bayesian updating (likelihood reasoning, likelihood ratio, Bayes factor)**
what_it_does: Revises the probability of a hypothesis in proportion to how much more likely the evidence is under it than under the alternatives. Artefact: a posterior probability or odds; read the likelihood ratio as the strength of the evidence.
fit_test: The prior or the likelihoods are guesses presented as precise numbers.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** No source was opened in this research.
purpose: Revises the probability of a hypothesis in proportion to how much more likely the evidence is under it than under alternatives and produces a posterior probability or odds.
use_when: Use when you hold a prior view on a hypothesis and need to say how far a piece of evidence should move it.
requires_minimum: A prior probability and the probability of each evidence item under each hypothesis.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the prior or the likelihoods are guesses presented as precise numbers. Treating dependent evidence items as independent overstates the posterior.
related_techniques: pairs with :: HE1-21 :: a base-rate check supplies defensible priors; substitutes for :: TC1-13 :: when evidence items can be given likelihoods as numbers (variable_types=ratio|counts or fractions)
typical_model_failure: States posterior probabilities to false precision from invented priors and likelihoods, or multiplies likelihoods of dependent evidence.

error_sources: input data; expert opinion; statistical assumptions
certainty_limits: Certainty is limited by the quality of the prior and the likelihoods, which are usually judgements. It drops further when evidence items are dependent or when the hypothesis set is incomplete (imprecision).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result gives a prior probability for the hypothesis, a likelihood of each evidence item under the hypothesis and under the alternatives, and the likelihood ratio for each item. It ends with a posterior probability or odds, with the likelihood ratio read as the strength of the evidence.

technique: **Disconfirmation search (falsification, seeking disconfirming evidence)**
what_it_does: Looks for evidence that would contradict a favoured claim. Artefact: a list of refuting evidence found or not found, with the search used.
fit_test: The search is shallow, or it is run after the conclusion is fixed.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Heuer's text states the aim of disproof within ACH; a primary source for the general technique was not opened, and no effect evidence was found. ([Heuer, Psychology of Intelligence Analysis](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Pyschology-of-Intelligence-Analysis.pdf))
purpose: Looks for evidence that would contradict a favoured claim and produces a list of refuting evidence found or not found with the search used.
use_when: Use when you hold a claim you believe and want to find out whether anything credible contradicts it before relying on it.
requires_minimum: A precisely stated claim and a statement, written before searching, of what evidence would refute it.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the search will be shallow or run after the conclusion is fixed. Not finding refuting evidence supports the claim only weakly.
related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-13 :: the surviving hypothesis is the claim to search against; pairs with :: CH-03 :: devil's advocacy builds the strongest opposing case from the same weak points
typical_model_failure: Searches with terms that favour the claim, stops after a few pages, and reports that no refuting evidence was found as if it confirmed the claim.
minimum_checks: exploratory:source-span citation; decision-informing:source-span citation; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:source-span citation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; source selection; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when the search is shallow, restricted to sources sharing the claim's origin, or run after the conclusion was fixed (risk of bias and reporting bias).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result names the claim under test, lists the evidence that would contradict it, and records for each item whether it was found or not found. It states the search used for each item and ends with what the findings mean for the claim.

technique: **Sensitivity analysis (robustness check, leave-one-out)**
what_it_does: Re-runs an analysis under different assumptions or inclusion rules. Artefact: a table of results by assumption; read whether the conclusion reverses.
fit_test: Only convenient assumptions are varied.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** The Cochrane Handbook advises it because meta-analysis results depend on many judgements. ([Cochrane Handbook, chapter 10](https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-10))
purpose: Re-runs an analysis under different assumptions or inclusion rules and produces a table of results by assumption showing whether the conclusion reverses.
use_when: Use when you want to know how much a result depends on the choices made in producing it.
requires_minimum: A completed analysis that can be re-run and a written list of the uncertain choices to vary.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when only convenient assumptions are varied. Agreement among variants of one analysis is consistency and not corroboration.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-06 :: varying pre-periods and controls tests the parallel trends assumption; pairs with :: TC1-18 :: sensitivity varies the choices and the consistency check tests the figures themselves
typical_model_failure: Varies only convenient assumptions and reports that the result holds, or changes several assumptions at once so the cause of a change is unclear.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:spot check; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; statistical assumptions; data transformation
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when only favourable alternatives are tried, when choices are not listed in advance, or when the original analysis is itself unsound.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table with one row per changed assumption or inclusion rule and the result obtained under each, alongside the original result. It ends by stating whether the conclusion reverses under any row.

what_it_does: Tests whether the claims, figures and assumptions within one analysis are compatible with each other. Artefact: a list of contradictions or inconsistent figures.
fit_test: Consistent results are read as correct (consistency does not show truth).
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** No source defines it as a named technique. Related documented checks are cross-consistency assessment in morphological analysis ([Wikipedia, Morphological analysis (problem-solving)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphological_analysis_(problem-solving))), dimensional checks (below) and coherence correction (above).

use_when: Use when you have a finished draft analysis and want to check that its numbers and statements do not contradict one another.
requires_minimum: A complete draft analysis with its figures and assumptions.
not_for_text: Misused when consistent results are read as correct, because consistency does not show truth.
related_techniques: pairs with :: CK-18 :: recomputation checks figures against the source while this check tests them against each other; pairs with :: TC1-28 :: unit checks catch contradictions that the figures hide
typical_model_failure: Misses contradictions that need arithmetic across tables, or reports an apparent contradiction that is only a difference in definitions.

what_it_does: Labels the parts of an argument: claim, ground, warrant, backing, rebuttal and qualifier. Artefact: a diagram per argument; a missing or unstated warrant is the likely point of error.
fit_test: The warrant is an unsupported generalisation, or the question that started the argument matters (the model does not cover it).
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described in argumentation theory; the model was based on legal arguments. ([Wikipedia, Toulmin model of argument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulmin_model_of_argument); [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Argument and argumentation](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/argument/))
purpose: Labels the parts of an argument as claim, ground, warrant, backing, rebuttal and qualifier and produces a diagram per argument.
use_when: Use when you need to see exactly what an argument rests on and which unstated step carries the weight.
requires_minimum: One written argument with a stated conclusion.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the warrant is an unsupported generalisation or when the question that started the argument matters, because the model does not cover it.
related_techniques: substitutes for :: TC1-20 :: when one argument is analysed in depth and not a debate among positions (unit_of_analysis=claim); pairs with :: TC1-21 :: fallacy checks need the argument in explicit form
typical_model_failure: Labels a restatement of the claim as its ground, or invents an unstated warrant that the author did not hold.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:source-span citation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:source-span citation; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; language model; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: The labelling describes structure only. Certainty drops where unstated warrants are inferred by the analyst and not found in the text.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a diagram for each argument labelling the claim, ground, warrant, backing, rebuttal and qualifier, with the text that fills each part. It names any missing or unstated warrant as the likely point of error.

technique: **Argument mapping (argument diagramming)**
what_it_does: Draws claims, reasons and objections as a diagram. Artefact: a diagram; read isolated claims and reasons that connect to no conclusion.
fit_test: The map needs many unstated links to connect its parts.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** A retrieved abstract claims that computer-based mapping gave gains more than three times those of other techniques, with no sample or statistics. use_when: Use when a long text or debate has many claims and you need to see how they connect and which have no support.
requires_minimum: A text or position containing at least one conclusion and its reasons.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the map needs many unstated links to connect its parts.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-19 :: Toulmin labelling examines the warrant of a single link that the map shows as a bare arrow; pairs with :: TC1-21 :: fallacy checks are applied to links the map makes explicit

error_sources: input data; language model; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: The map describes structure and not truth. Certainty drops when links are inferred and not stated in the text.

output_spec: The result is a diagram of the claims, reasons and objections, with the links between them showing what supports or opposes what and which claim is the main conclusion. It names the isolated claims and the reasons that connect to no conclusion.

technique: **Fallacy analysis (informal fallacies, pragma-dialectical rules)**
what_it_does: Compares an argument with a list or rule set of known defective patterns. Artefact: a list of suspected defects; read each as a prompt for missing support, not as proof of falsity.
fit_test: A label is applied to a plausible argument because it resembles a pattern.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** The Stanford Encyclopedia records critiques: Hamblin on textbook treatment, Massey that no argument can be shown fallacious on purely logical grounds, and Johnson that the appearance condition is subjective. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/))
purpose: Compares an argument with a list of known defective patterns and produces a list of suspected defects, each read as a prompt for missing support.
use_when: Use when an argument sounds convincing and you want to check whether it relies on a recognised faulty pattern of reasoning.
requires_minimum: An argument stated in explicit form, with premises and conclusion separated.
not_for_text: Misused when a label is applied to a plausible argument because it resembles a pattern. A label is a prompt for missing support and not proof that the conclusion is false.
related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-19 :: the argument must first be set out in explicit form; should follow :: TC1-20 :: the map makes the links to be checked visible
typical_model_failure: Applies a fallacy name to a sound argument because it resembles the pattern and presents the label as a refutation.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:source-span citation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:source-span citation; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; language model; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Labels are prompts and not proof of falsity. Certainty drops where a label depends on a subjective judgement of how the argument appears.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a list of suspected defects, each giving the passage of the argument, the named fallacy or rule broken, and the support that appears to be missing. It states that each entry is a prompt for missing support and not proof that the claim is false.

technique: **Abduction and inference to the best explanation**
what_it_does: Ranks candidate explanations of an observation and selects the best. Artefact: ranked explanations scored on simplicity, generality and coherence; a close tie signals the need for discriminating evidence.
fit_test: Only poorly supported rivals were considered (the bad lot objection).
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described, with objections including underdetermination and circularity. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Abduction](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/abduction/))
purpose: Ranks candidate explanations of an observation on simplicity, generality and coherence and produces a ranked list of explanations.
use_when: Use when you have an observation and several possible explanations and need to pick the best one or see that two are tied.
requires_minimum: Evidence and at least two rival explanations, with the criteria for ranking stated beforehand.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when only poorly supported rivals were considered (the bad lot objection). A close tie means discriminating evidence is needed and not that either explanation is true.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-16 :: a close tie needs discriminating evidence found by a targeted search; pairs with :: TC1-13 :: the matrix tests the leading explanations against all evidence
typical_model_failure: Picks the most vivid or familiar explanation and does not generate serious rivals.

error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; expert opinion
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when the set of rivals is poor, when evidence underdetermines the choice, or when the criteria weights are not stated (risk of bias and indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a ranked list of candidate explanations of the observation, with a score for each on simplicity, generality and coherence. It names the best explanation and says whether a close tie means that discriminating evidence is needed.

technique: **Ladder of inference**
what_it_does: Traces how a conclusion was reached, from observed data through selected data and interpretation to belief. Artefact: a stepwise list; the step where data selection or interpretation was added is the likely error.
fit_test: A conclusion cannot be linked to observed data.
status_and_evidence: **Practice.** Attributed to Argyris; the page gives no rungs, evidence or criticism. ([Wikipedia, Ladder of inference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladder_of_inference))
purpose: Traces how a conclusion was reached from observed data through selected data and interpretation to belief and produces a stepwise list.
use_when: Use when a conclusion seems firmly held and you want to find the step where data were selected or interpreted that may have introduced an error.
requires_minimum: A stated conclusion and an account of the data behind it.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when a conclusion cannot be linked to any observed data. The reconstruction is a prompt for inquiry and not evidence of bias.
related_techniques: pairs with :: CH-13 :: bias checks name the judgement biases at the rungs where selection happened; pairs with :: CH-12 :: Socratic questions elicit the account of the data and reasoning
typical_model_failure: Reconstructs a plausible ladder after the fact that the author did not follow, and attributes data selection to bias without evidence.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:source-span citation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:source-span citation; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; language model
certainty_limits: The ladder is a reconstruction of reasoning and describes it only. Certainty drops when the account of the data is supplied by the person whose reasoning is traced.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a stepwise list from the observed data, through the data selected and the interpretation added, to the belief held, with the content of each step written out. It names the step where data selection or interpretation was added as the likely error.

technique: **Reflective equilibrium**
what_it_does: Adjusts principles and case judgements against each other until they cohere. Artefact: a revised set of principles and judgements; the judgements dropped show where theory and intuition conflict.
fit_test: Only coherence is achieved, with no independent support from background theories.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Criticisms include conflicting equilibria between people and indeterminate results. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Reflective equilibrium](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/reflective-equilibrium/))
purpose: Adjusts principles and case judgements against each other until they cohere and produces a revised set of principles and judgements.
use_when: Use when your general principles and your judgements about specific cases conflict and you need to work out which to revise.
requires_minimum: Considered judgements on specific cases, candidate principles and the background theories that bear on them.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when only coherence is achieved with no independent support from background theories. Different people can reach conflicting equilibria, and results can be indeterminate.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-26 :: thought experiments supply the case judgements to be reconciled; pairs with :: TC1-25 :: first principles reasoning supplies candidate base principles
typical_model_failure: Adjusts the principles until they fit the judgements it was given, producing coherence with no independent support.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: coder or rater judgement; expert opinion; language model
certainty_limits: The result shows coherence only. Certainty drops when judgements come from one person or when background theories are not consulted (risk of bias).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result lists the principles and case judgements before and after adjustment and gives a revised set of both that cohere. It names the judgements that were dropped, since they show where theory and intuition conflict.

technique: **First principles reasoning**
what_it_does: Replaces inherited convention with a derivation from basic premises. Artefact: a derivation chain; the premises at its base are the assumptions the whole result depends on.
fit_test: The choice of base premises is itself contested, so the derivation only shifts the dispute.
status_and_evidence: **Practice.** The popular management use is not evaluated on the source page. ([Wikipedia, First principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_principle))
purpose: Replaces inherited convention with a derivation from basic premises and produces a derivation chain with the base premises listed as assumptions.
use_when: Use when a conclusion rests on convention and you want to rebuild it from premises that everyone accepts.
requires_minimum: A disputed conclusion and base premises accepted by all parties to the dispute.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the choice of base premises is itself contested, because the derivation then only shifts the dispute.
related_techniques: pairs with :: CH-01 :: a key assumptions check tests the premises at the base of the derivation; pairs with :: TC1-24 :: reflective equilibrium tests the derived result against case judgements
typical_model_failure: Treats conventions as basic premises and derives a result that restates them.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:expert review; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: coder or rater judgement; expert opinion; language model
certainty_limits: The result is only as secure as the base premises. Certainty drops when premises are contested or when the derivation has steps that are not shown.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a derivation chain from basic premises to the conclusion, with each step following from the one before it. It has a register of the premises at the base of the chain, which are the assumptions the whole result depends on.

technique: **Thought experiments**
what_it_does: Constructs an imagined case to test a principle. Artefact: a judgement about the case, which is evidence about the principle only if reasoners agree.
fit_test: Details of the case, not the principle, determine the judgement.
status_and_evidence: **Unconfirmed.** The source entry failed to load, so no claim was verified.
purpose: Constructs an imagined case to test a principle and produces a judgement about the case that counts as evidence on the principle only if reasoners agree.
use_when: Use when a principle cannot be tested on real cases and you want to see whether it gives acceptable answers in a constructed one.
requires_minimum: A principle to test and a constructed case that isolates the feature of interest.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when details of the case, and not the principle, determine the judgement.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-24 :: reflective equilibrium reconciles the case judgement with the principle
typical_model_failure: Builds a case whose incidental details produce the judgement and counts the model's own reaction as evidence about the principle.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:spot check; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: coder or rater judgement; expert opinion; language model
certainty_limits: A judgement from one reasoner is weak evidence. Certainty drops when reasoners disagree or when the result changes with details of the case.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result describes the imagined case, states the principle it tests and gives the judgement about the case. It notes whether the reasoners agree, since the judgement is evidence about the principle only if they do.

technique: **Fermi estimation and order-of-magnitude checks (back-of-the-envelope estimate)**
what_it_does: Breaks an unknown quantity into factors that can be estimated and multiplies them. Artefact: a number with a plausible range, used as a bound on a detailed result.
fit_test: Independent routes differ by more than an order of magnitude, or they share a bias, so errors do not cancel.
status_and_evidence: **Tested.** Tested for teaching only: a classroom study reported medium effects on transfer, with difficulties in units and notation. No test of research accuracy was found. ([Wikipedia, Fermi problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi_problem); [arXiv 2405.16480, teaching estimation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.16480))
purpose: Breaks an unknown quantity into factors that can be estimated, multiplies them, and produces a number with a plausible range used as a bound on a detailed result.
use_when: Use when you need to know quickly whether a figure is the right order of magnitude or to bound a quantity that has no direct data.
requires_minimum: A quantity that can be split into at least two factors with rough values and units. Two independent routes are preferred.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when independent routes differ by more than an order of magnitude, or when they share a bias so that errors do not cancel.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-28 :: unit checks confirm that the factors multiply to the right units; pairs with :: HE1-21 :: base-rate and distribution checks supply the rough factor values
typical_model_failure: Multiplies factors with inconsistent units or correlated errors and reports the product to more precision than the inputs allow.
minimum_checks: exploratory:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:sensitivity analysis; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:sensitivity analysis; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; statistical assumptions; expert opinion
certainty_limits: The estimate is a bound and not a measurement. Certainty drops when the routes share a bias or when factor values are guesses with no source.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result lists the factors the unknown quantity is broken into, an estimate for each and the product of those estimates. It ends with a number and a plausible range, stated as a bound against a detailed result.

technique: **Dimensional and unit checks**
what_it_does: Checks that both sides of a relation have the same units. Artefact: a unit balance; a mismatch indicates an error in the derivation.
fit_test: A match is read as proof; numerical factors are invisible to the check.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described on an encyclopaedia page. ([Wikipedia, Dimensional analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimensional_analysis))
purpose: Checks that both sides of a relation have the same units and produces a unit balance in which a mismatch flags an error in the derivation.
use_when: Use when a formula or calculation has been produced and you want to catch errors in its units before relying on the number.
requires_minimum: A formula or calculation with units attached to every quantity.
not_for_text: Misused when a match is read as proof. Numerical factors are invisible to the check.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC1-27 :: an order-of-magnitude check catches numerical factors that a unit check cannot see; pairs with :: TC1-18 :: the consistency check covers contradictions between figures
typical_model_failure: Treats a matching unit balance as proof of correctness, or overlooks mixed units such as per cent against percentage points.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; data transformation
certainty_limits: A match shows only that units agree. Logic errors and wrong numerical factors remain unchecked.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table with one row per relation, giving the units on each side and the unit balance for the relation. It lists any mismatch as an error in the derivation, and says where the mismatch occurs.

technique: GRIM test (granularity-related inconsistency of means)
what_it_does: Checks whether a reported mean of whole-number data can arise from the reported sample size. Artefact: a flag for possible or impossible means. Read a flag as a reporting error to query, not as proof of misconduct.
fit_test: Fits whole-number data such as Likert items with small samples. Misfit: non-integer data, or large samples where many means are possible. Needs the reported sample size and item count.
status_and_evidence: Documented. In a preprint, 71 of 260 psychology articles were testable and 36 of those 71 (50.7 per cent) had at least one inconsistent mean. ([Brown and Heathers, PeerJ preprint 2064](https://peerj.com/preprints/2064))
purpose: Checks whether a reported mean of whole-number data can arise from the reported sample size and item count and produces a flag for possible or impossible means.
use_when: Use when a report gives means from whole-number scales such as Likert items and you want to know whether they are arithmetically possible.
requires_minimum: A reported mean with its decimals, the sample size and the number of items, for whole-number data. Most informative when sample size times item count is small.
not_for_text: Wrong choice for non-integer data, or for large samples where nearly every mean is possible. A flag is a reporting error to query and not proof of misconduct.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC-03 :: statcheck tests the reported test statistics while this test checks the reported means; should follow :: CK-18 :: recomputation of reported figures confirms that the numbers were extracted correctly
typical_model_failure: Applies the test to data that are not whole numbers or ignores rounding rules, and reports false inconsistencies.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:spot check; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; data transformation
certainty_limits: A flag can come from rounding, a typing error or missing participants and does not show misconduct. Certainty drops when the sample size or item count is not stated.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table with one row per reported mean, giving the mean, the sample size and a flag of possible or impossible. It states that a flag is a reporting error to query and not proof of misconduct.

technique: SPRITE (Sample Parameter Reconstruction via Iterative TEchniques)
what_it_does: Reconstructs possible datasets that match reported descriptive statistics. Artefact: plausible samples. Read the range of possible distributions of item values.
fit_test: The abstract does not state the inputs; mean, standard deviation, sample size and scale range are assumed. Code exists in MATLAB, R and Python.
status_and_evidence: Documented. Description only, from a preprint. ([Heathers et al., PeerJ preprint 26968](https://peerj.com/preprints/26968))
purpose: Reconstructs possible datasets that match reported descriptive statistics and produces plausible samples showing the range of possible item distributions.
use_when: Use when a report gives only a mean, standard deviation and sample size and you want to know what data could have produced them.
requires_minimum: Reported mean, standard deviation, sample size and scale range for each reconstructed measure.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when any of the four inputs is missing or when the measure is not a bounded scale. A reconstructed sample shows only that data are possible and is not the real data.
related_techniques: should follow :: TC-01 :: the mean must first be shown to be possible; pairs with :: TC-03 :: statcheck tests the reported test statistics that depend on the same descriptives
typical_model_failure: Presents one reconstructed sample as the real data, or accepts a sample that breaks the scale limits.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:spot check; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; statistical assumptions
certainty_limits: Many samples fit the same statistics, so a reconstruction shows possibility and not what happened. Certainty drops when rounding is unknown or the scale range is unstated.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result gives the reported descriptive statistics, and one or more plausible samples that match them, each listing the item values. It ends with the range of possible distributions of item values across the samples.

technique: statcheck (recomputation of reported p-values)
what_it_does: Recomputes p-values from reported test statistics and degrees of freedom and flags mismatches. Artefact: a list of inconsistencies and gross inconsistencies, where a gross inconsistency changes the significance decision at the 0.05 level.
fit_test: Fits text with results in American Psychological Association style. Misfit: tables, other formats, or results with an effect size between statistic and p-value. It cannot tell which element is wrong.
status_and_evidence: Tested. It extracted 67.5 per cent of results found by hand in a 49-article validation and may overstate inconsistencies (9.0 against 4.3 per cent by hand). Across 30,717 articles, 49.6 per cent of those with such results had at least one inconsistency and 12.9 per cent at least one gross inconsistency. ([Nuijten et al., Behavior Research Methods 2016](https://rd.springer.com/content/pdf/10.3758/s13428-015-0664-2.pdf))
purpose: Recomputes p-values from reported test statistics and degrees of freedom and produces a list of inconsistencies and gross inconsistencies.
use_when: Use when you want to check that the p-values in a set of articles match their reported test statistics.
requires_minimum: Test statistics, degrees of freedom and p-values reported in American Psychological Association style text.
not_for_text: Wrong choice for results in tables or other formats, or where an effect size sits between the statistic and the p-value. It cannot tell which element is wrong, and it may overstate inconsistencies (9.0 against 4.3 per cent by hand).
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC-01 :: GRIM checks reported means while statcheck checks reported test statistics; pairs with :: CK-18 :: recomputation of figures covers numbers outside the test statistic format
typical_model_failure: Misses results that are not in the expected format and reports a mismatch caused by rounding or a one-sided test as an error.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:spot check; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; data transformation
certainty_limits: A mismatch can come from rounding, one-sided tests or typing errors. The software extracted 67.5 per cent of results found by hand, so a clean result covers only the extracted part.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a list of reported tests, each with the test statistic, degrees of freedom, the reported p-value and the recomputed p-value. It marks each inconsistency, and marks as gross the ones where the significance decision changes at the 0.05 level.

technique: Claim and citation verification against source text (fact verification; claim checking; citation support check; quotation accuracy check)
what_it_does: Labels a claim as supported, refuted or not enough information against retrieved evidence, or checks that a cited source supports the claim it is attached to. Artefact: a label with evidence sentences, or a supported, minor-error or major-error rating per citation. Read the evidence sentences, and read repeated claims for a shared origin.
fit_test: Fits when the corpus or cited source contains the relevant sentence. Misfit: evidence spread across documents or needing inference, paywalled sources, and opinions or predictions extracted as claims. The minor-error class is subjective (kappa of 0.26 in one study).
status_and_evidence: Tested. A 2018 baseline pipeline reached 31.87 per cent accuracy even with correct evidence supplied, and annotators agreed at Fleiss kappa 0.6841 (not a statement about current models). A meta-analysis of 28 medical studies gave a pooled citation error rate of 25.4 per cent, with 11.9 per cent major errors. ([Thorne et al., FEVER, arXiv 1803.05355](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.05355); [Jergas and Baethge, PeerJ 2015](https://peerj.com/articles/1364))
purpose: Labels each claim as supported, refuted or not enough information against retrieved evidence, or rates whether a cited source supports its claim, and produces a label with evidence sentences.
use_when: Use when you need to check whether claims in a text, or the sources cited for them, are actually backed by the source text.
requires_minimum: Claims in separable form and the cited source or an evidence corpus that contains the relevant passage.
not_for_text: Wrong choice when evidence is spread across documents or needs inference, the source is paywalled, or the claims extracted are opinions or predictions. The minor-error class is subjective (kappa of 0.26 in one study).
related_techniques: should follow :: CK-19 :: atomic claim decomposition splits the text into the claims to be checked; pairs with :: CK-17 :: a string match by code confirms that each cited passage exists; pairs with :: IS-06 :: repeated claims may share one origin and so do not corroborate each other
typical_model_failure: Labels a claim as supported because a similar sentence exists, and counts a claim repeated across sources as independently confirmed.
minimum_checks: exploratory:source-span citation; decision-informing:source-span citation; decision-informing:human review sample; high-stakes:source-span citation; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:gold standard agreement; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; language model; source selection; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when evidence is spread across documents, needs inference or is behind a paywall, when labels are judged subjectively, and when repeated claims share one origin (inconsistency and indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table with one row per claim or citation, giving the claim, the source, the label (supported, refuted or not enough information, or a supported, minor-error or major-error rating) and the evidence sentences behind it. It names the repeated claims that share an origin.

technique: Subgroup and Simpson's paradox check (stratified reanalysis; confounding check; collapsibility check)
what_it_does: Recomputes an association within subgroups to see whether the pooled direction reverses or vanishes. Artefact: pooled and stratified estimates side by side. Read for a change of sign. In the encyclopaedia example, recovery was 50 per cent in treated and untreated groups overall, yet 61 against 57 per cent in men and 44 against 40 per cent in women.
fit_test: Run whenever aggregate rates are compared across groups of unequal composition. Which partition to trust depends on causal structure, not on the numbers, and conditioning on a mediator distorts the effect.
status_and_evidence: Documented. Different partitions of the same data can support incompatible causal conclusions. ([Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Simpson's paradox](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/paradox-simpson/); [Stanford Encyclopedia: Simpson's paradox (2006 archive)](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2006/entries/paradox-simpson/))
purpose: Recomputes an association within subgroups to see whether the pooled direction reverses or vanishes and produces pooled and stratified estimates side by side.
use_when: Use when aggregate rates are compared across groups of unequal composition and you want to see whether the pattern holds inside each group.
requires_minimum: A pooled comparison, a grouping variable plausibly related to both exposure and outcome, and enough records in each subgroup to estimate the association.
not_for_text: Misused when the stratified result is trusted without asking which partition fits the causal structure. Conditioning on a mediator distorts the effect.
related_techniques: should follow :: TC1-08 :: the graph decides which partition to trust; pairs with :: TC-06 :: the ecological check asks whether group-level results apply to individuals
typical_model_failure: Reports the stratified result as the true effect without asking which partition fits the causal structure, or stratifies on a mediator.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:sensitivity analysis; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:sensitivity analysis; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; statistical assumptions; data transformation
certainty_limits: The correct partition depends on causal structure outside the data. Certainty drops when strata are small or the grouping variable is a mediator or collider (risk of bias and imprecision).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table giving the pooled estimate and the estimate within each subgroup, side by side. It states whether the direction changes sign or the association vanishes in the subgroups.

technique: Ecological fallacy check (aggregation bias check)
what_it_does: Decides whether a claim about people is supported by group-level data. Artefact: a decision on whether the claim is group-level or individual-level. In Robinson's 1930 state data the correlation between illiteracy and foreign-born share was about minus 0.53, against about plus 0.12 for individuals.
fit_test: Fits claims about people drawn from regional, organisational or document-level aggregates. Misfit: individual-level data are available, and then they should be used. The reverse error was not covered.
status_and_evidence: Documented. Read on an encyclopaedia page citing Robinson (1950); the original was not opened. ([Wikipedia: Ecological fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecological_fallacy))
purpose: Decides whether a claim about people is supported by group-level data and produces a decision on whether the claim is group-level or individual-level.
use_when: Use when a claim about individuals is drawn from regional, organisational or document-level aggregates.
requires_minimum: A claim about individuals and the group-level data it was drawn from.
not_for_rules: access_depth=record-level :: individual-level data are available and should be used instead
not_for_text: The reverse error, where individual patterns are wrongly applied to groups, is not covered.
related_techniques: pairs with :: TC-05 :: subgroup reanalysis shows whether a pooled pattern reverses inside groups; pairs with :: TC1-08 :: a causal graph states at which level the mechanism acts
typical_model_failure: Reads a group-level correlation as a statement about individuals, or fails to notice that the claim concerns people when the data are regional.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:alternative explanations check; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: The decision depends on how the claim is worded and what the unit of the data is. Certainty drops when the data level is not documented.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result states the claim, the level of the data (group or individual) and the level of the claim. It ends with a decision on whether the claim is group-level or individual-level and whether the group-level data supports it.

technique: **Admiralty system (source reliability and information credibility grading)**
what_it_does: Gives each report a two-character grade, rating the source (A to F) and the information (1 to 6) separately. Artefact: a code such as B2; read the letter as the source's history and the number as how well the item is corroborated.
fit_test: The source is new, anonymous or has no comparators (default F and 6). The grades are ordinal, and reliability from past performance does not predict a new claim.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Read on a secondary page citing UK and US military publications; the primary document was not opened. ([Wikipedia, Admiralty code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiralty_code))
purpose: Assigns each report a two-character grade for source reliability (A to F) and information credibility (1 to 6) and produces an appraised evidence base.
use_when: Use when you need to say how far to trust each report from a source with a known track record, and whether other independent reports back it.
requires_minimum: none
not_for_text: The source is new or anonymous with no comparators, so the default grade F6 carries no information. Do not read a grade from past performance as a prediction about a new claim.
related_techniques: pairs with :: HE1-06 :: the information grade depends on corroboration, which triangulation tests; pairs with :: IS-06 :: copy detection stops copied reports from raising the information grade
typical_model_failure: Assigns a letter grade from the tone of the report instead of the source's record, or scores information credibility without checking whether the corroborating reports are independent.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:human review sample; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; source selection
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when the track record is thin, when corroborating reports copy each other (inconsistency and risk of bias) and when grades are read as more than ordinal.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table with one row per report, giving a two-character grade such as B2, where the letter (A to F) rates the source and the number (1 to 6) rates the information. It states what each grade rests on, the source's history for the letter and the corroboration for the number.

technique: **Quality of information check**
what_it_does: Rates the completeness, accuracy and corroboration of each source. Artefact: a source database and a statement of what is known and unknown; read items with single-source support.
fit_test: The output is a count of sources, not an assessment of each. Many sources do not replace thoroughly examined good information.
status_and_evidence: **Documented.** Described in the CIA primer without effect evidence. Equivalence to the PHIA 'Analytical Confidence Method' is unconfirmed because that document does not describe the method. ([CIA Tradecraft Primer (2009)](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Tradecraft-Primer-apr09.pdf); [UK PHIA Professional Development Framework (2019)](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6421b6a43d885d000fdadb70/2019-01_PHIA_PDF_First_Edition_Electronic_Distribution_v1.1__1_.pdf))
purpose: Rates the completeness, accuracy and corroboration of each source and produces a source database with a statement of what is known and unknown.
use_when: Use when you need to know which parts of the evidence rest on a single source and how much of the picture is missing.
requires_minimum: none
not_for_text: The output is only a count of sources. Many sources do not replace a few thoroughly examined good ones.
related_techniques: pairs with :: HE1-01 :: the grade adds a source reliability letter to this completeness and accuracy rating
typical_model_failure: Rates completeness against what the model already knows instead of against the question, and treats the number of sources as quality.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:human review sample; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; source selection
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when ratings rest on one assessor, when sources are not independent, or when excluded reporting was never reviewed (reporting bias).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
