technique: Inter-coder agreement statistics (percentage agreement; Cohen's kappa; weighted kappa; Scott's pi; Fleiss' kappa; Krippendorff's alpha; intercoder reliability testing)
what_it_does: Measures how far coders, human or model, give the same code to the same items, corrected for chance. Artefact: a coefficient per code, with a bootstrap interval. Read each code separately, not only the overall figure, and read the category distribution beside it.
fit_test: Cohen's kappa suits exactly two coders. Scott's pi, Fleiss' kappa and Krippendorff's alpha extend to more coders, and alpha also handles missing codes and ordinal or numeric codes. Percentage agreement is an upper bound because it includes chance agreement. Skewed categories make kappa hard to interpret.
status_and_evidence: Documented. Alpha has no universal cutoff. Krippendorff's conventions, reported secondhand, are 0.8 for serious purposes and 0.67 as a tentative lower bound. Artstein and Poesio advise at least three coders and bootstrap intervals. ([Hayes and Krippendorff 2007](https://www.asc.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/2021-03/Answering%20the%20Call%20for%20a%20Standard%20Reliability%20Measure%20for%20Coding%20Data.pdf); [Artstein and Poesio 2008, Inter-coder agreement for computational linguistics](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1516/R216/Artstein.pdf); [Krippendorff, Computing Krippendorff alpha-reliability (abstract)](https://repository.upenn.edu/asc_papers/43))
purpose: Measure how far coders, human or model, give the same code to the same items, corrected for chance, and produce an agreement coefficient per code with a bootstrap interval in a validation report.
use_when: Use when two or more coders have coded the same items and you need to know whether the coding is reliable enough to use.
requires_minimum: at least two coders on the same items, at least 50 items overall and enough items in each code to estimate agreement
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the model is scored against itself and treated as another independent coder. Skewed category distributions make kappa hard to read, and percentage agreement overstates reliability.
related_techniques: should follow :: MM-08 :: model codes are one of the coder sets compared; should follow :: CK-04 :: the human-coded set gives the human coders; pairs with :: CK-03 :: bootstrap intervals show the precision of each coefficient
typical_model_failure: Scores the model against itself and not against humans, or treats the model as one more independent coder though its errors are correlated across items.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; statistical assumptions
certainty_limits: Certainty drops with few coders or items (imprecision), skewed categories (indirectness) and coders who were not independent (risk of bias).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table with one row per code, giving the agreement coefficient, its bootstrap interval and the category distribution for that code. It also gives the overall figure and names the codes with the lowest agreement.

technique: Model versus human coding agreement protocol (LLM-as-coder reliability test; intra-coder agreement across runs)
what_it_does: Scores the model as one coder against a human coder or panel, and against itself across repeated runs. Artefact: human-human agreement (the upper limit), model-human agreement and model-model agreement. Read the model-human figure against the human-human figure, not against 1.
fit_test: Needs an acceptable human-human baseline. Misfit: the humans disagree with each other as much as with the model, so the task is under-specified. High self-agreement does not show accuracy.
status_and_evidence: Tested. ChatGPT agreed with itself across runs more than crowd workers and trained annotators did on all tasks (2023). Another study found consistency fell short of accepted reliability thresholds on a news classification task (2023). ([Gilardi et al., arXiv 2303.15056](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15056); [Reiss, arXiv 2304.11085](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11085))
purpose: Score a model as one coder against a human coder or panel and against itself across repeated runs, and produce human-human, model-human and model-model agreement in a validation report.
use_when: Use when a language model has coded text and you need to know if it agrees with humans as well as humans agree with each other.
requires_minimum: at least two human coders on a shared sample, a human-human baseline and at least three repeated model runs
not_for_text: Wrong choice when humans disagree with each other as much as with the model, because the task is then under-specified. High self-agreement across runs does not show accuracy.
related_techniques: should follow :: MM-08 :: the model codes are what is tested; should follow :: CK-04 :: the human-coded sample gives the human baseline; pairs with :: CK-01 :: agreement coefficients give the human-human baseline; pairs with :: CK-10 :: repeated-run tests cover self-agreement in more detail
typical_model_failure: Consistent but wrong labels pass a self-agreement test.

output_spec: The result reports three agreement figures: human-human agreement as the upper limit, model-human agreement and model-model agreement across repeated runs. It states the model-human figure as a comparison with the human-human figure and says whether the humans agree with each other well enough to serve as a baseline.

technique: Bootstrap confidence intervals for agreement and accuracy (bootstrap resampling of items)
what_it_does: Quantifies sampling uncertainty in a reliability or accuracy figure computed from a finite review sample, by resampling items. Artefact: an interval around the coefficient. Read the lower bound against the threshold needed.
fit_test: Needs independent items. Clustered items, such as many snippets from one document, need cluster resampling (inference). Small samples give wide intervals.
status_and_evidence: Documented. The source recommends bootstrapping for alpha and reporting confidence intervals. General bootstrap theory was not opened. ([Artstein and Poesio 2008, Inter-coder agreement for computational linguistics](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1516/R216/Artstein.pdf))
purpose: Quantify sampling uncertainty in an agreement or accuracy figure computed from a review sample by resampling items, and produce an interval around the coefficient.
use_when: Use when you have an agreement or accuracy figure from a small review sample and need to know how precise it is.
requires_minimum: at least 30 independent reviewed items
not_for_text: Wrong choice when items are clustered, such as many snippets from one document, unless clusters are resampled. Small samples give wide intervals that must not be hidden.
related_techniques: should follow :: CK-01 :: the coefficient needs an interval; should follow :: CK-24 :: the review sample design sets how items were drawn; pairs with :: CK-04 :: gold-standard accuracy figures need intervals
typical_model_failure: Reports an interval without computing it, which gives invented precision.

certainty_limits: Certainty drops when items are not independent (risk of bias) and when the reviewed sample is small (imprecision).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result gives, for each reliability or accuracy figure, the point value and its bootstrap interval, with the sample size beside it. It states whether the lower bound of each interval meets the threshold needed.

technique: Gold-standard validation sample (ground truth set; human-coded validation set)
what_it_does: Builds a human-coded random or stratified subset against which model output is scored. Artefact: a labelled set. Read agreement among the human coders first.
fit_test: Needs categories that humans can apply. Misfit: humans cannot produce the measure reliably. Revise the codebook after ambiguities, and recheck the set with agreement statistics.
status_and_evidence: Documented. The source states that "no statistical model can repair a poorly constructed training set" and quotes about 500 documents as a rule of thumb, with 100 "probably being enough". ([Grimmer and Stewart 2013, Political Analysis](https://web.stanford.edu/~jgrimmer/tad2.pdf))
purpose: Build a random or stratified human-coded subset against which model output is scored and produce a labelled set.
use_when: Use when you need human-made labels to test or tune a model or codebook and have none yet.
requires_minimum: about 100 items at the least, and about 500 documents where categories are many or rare, from Grimmer and Stewart
not_for_text: Wrong choice when humans cannot apply the categories reliably. A model must not be used to build the gold set, or the check will share the output's errors.
related_techniques: pairs with :: CK-01 :: agreement statistics test whether the human coders agree; pairs with :: CK-24 :: the sample design controls how items are drawn
typical_model_failure: Uses a model to build the gold set, so the errors in the check match the errors in the output.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:human review sample; decision-informing:gold standard agreement; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:gold standard agreement; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; source selection
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when coders disagree (risk of bias), when the sample is not random or stratified (indirectness) and when it is small (imprecision).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a labelled set of items drawn at random or by stratum, with one row per item showing the item and the code each human coder gave it. It reports agreement among the human coders and lists the items on which they disagreed.

technique: Out-of-sample validation (train and test split; k-fold cross-validation; bootstrap; permutation test)
what_it_does: Tunes prompts, rules or models on one set of items and scores them on another. Artefact: out-of-sample error, interval or null distribution. Read the gap between training and test results.
fit_test: Use for any model or any pattern found by search. Random splits leak when items are near-duplicates or share a source (inference).
status_and_evidence: Documented. In V-fold cross-validation all predictions are made on data out of sample. Cross-validation documentation was not opened. ([Grimmer and Stewart 2013, Political Analysis](https://web.stanford.edu/~jgrimmer/tad2.pdf))
purpose: Tune prompts, rules or models on one set of items and score them on a held-out set, and produce an out-of-sample error, interval or null distribution in a validation report.
use_when: Use when a model or a pattern found by search needs an honest estimate of how it performs on items it has not seen.
requires_minimum: enough items that both the training and the held-out part support an error estimate, usually several hundred
not_for_text: Wrong choice when items are near-duplicates or share a source, because a random split then leaks. Reporting training performance, or reporting the best of many tested patterns, is a misuse.

produces: validation report:complete; result:validated; held-out test sample:opened

technique: Bias correction of model labels with a human-coded subsample (design-based supervised learning (DSL); prediction-powered inference (PPI); regression estimator correction)
what_it_does: Combines model labels for all items with human labels for a random subsample, so that downstream estimates and intervals stay valid. Artefact: a corrected estimate with an interval. Read whether the conclusion survives the correction.
fit_test: Fits when model labels are used in a numeric claim or comparison. Misfit: no random human-coded subsample with known sampling probabilities. Correction trades Type I against Type II error.
status_and_evidence: Tested. Using surrogate labels directly gave substantial bias and invalid confidence intervals even when labels were 80 to 90 per cent accurate (2023). Prediction-powered inference gives valid intervals with no assumption about the prediction model (2023, abstract). ([Egami et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.04746](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.04746); [Angelopoulos et al. 2023, arXiv 2301.09633](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.09633); [Baumann et al. 2025, arXiv 2509.08825](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08825))
purpose: Combine model labels for all items with human labels for a random subsample so that downstream estimates and intervals stay valid, and produce a corrected estimate with an interval.
use_when: Use when model-generated labels are used in a numeric claim or a regression and you need estimates that are not biased by label errors.
requires_minimum: a random human-coded subsample with known sampling probabilities, usually a few hundred items
not_for_text: Wrong choice when there is no random human-coded subsample with known probabilities. The correction trades Type I against Type II error and does not repair a badly defined category.
related_techniques: should follow :: MM-08 :: model labels for all items are the input; should follow :: CK-04 :: the random human-coded subsample is the correction set; pairs with :: CK-12 :: a specification sweep shows how far conclusions depend on label choices
typical_model_failure: Counts model labels as truth in a regression, or reports uncorrected label counts as population values.

tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result gives a corrected estimate with its interval, set beside the uncorrected estimate from the model labels alone. It states the size of the human-coded subsample and whether the conclusion survives the correction.

technique: Split-sample design for measures discovered from text (split-sample framework)
what_it_does: Discovers the measure (categories or topics) in one random part of the corpus and estimates the effect in the other. Artefact: an effect estimate that does not overfit the discovery. Read whether the effect persists in the estimation sample.
fit_test: Fits when a text-derived measure is the treatment or outcome in a causal claim. Only the abstract was read.
status_and_evidence: Documented. Estimating the latent representation on the same data "may introduce an identification problem or overfit" (2018). ([Egami et al. 2018, arXiv 1802.02163](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.02163))
purpose: Discover a measure such as categories or topics in one random part of the corpus and estimate its effect in the other, and produce an effect estimate that does not overfit the discovery.
use_when: Use when a measure found in text will be used as a treatment or outcome in an effect or comparison claim.
requires_minimum: enough documents to split into a discovery part and an estimation part, each large enough for its task
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the categories are discovered and tested on the same documents. Only the abstract of the source was read, so the design details are unconfirmed.

technique: Semantic, predictive and convergent validity checks (construct validity checks)
what_it_does: Tests whether an extracted category or measure behaves as the concept it claims to measure. Artefact: raters' verdicts on pairs of items, and comparisons with a known event or an established measure. Read agreement with the benchmark.
fit_test: Needs an external benchmark. Misfit: the benchmark is derived from the same model, or measures something related but different. Semantic validity is human rating of coherence, predictive validity is movement with expected events, and convergent validity is agreement with an established measure.
status_and_evidence: Documented. Worked examples include raters judging document pairs and topic use against committee jurisdiction. ([Grimmer and Stewart 2013, Political Analysis](https://web.stanford.edu/~jgrimmer/tad2.pdf))
purpose: Test whether an extracted category or measure behaves as the concept it claims to measure, and produce rater verdicts and comparisons with a known event or established measure in a validation report.
use_when: Use when a topic, theme or score from text needs evidence that it means what you say it means.
requires_minimum: an external benchmark and enough raters or item pairs to judge agreement
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the benchmark comes from the same model or measures something related but different. Semantic validity is human rating of coherence, and the other two types need an outside measure.

It names the benchmark used and states whether the category or measure behaves as the concept it claims to measure.

technique: Cluster validation indexes (silhouette score; adjusted Rand index; adjusted mutual information; V-measure; stability analysis)
what_it_does: Scores how well a clustering fits the data or agrees with known labels. Artefact: a score per clustering. Read relative to alternatives such as other numbers of clusters.

not_for_text: Wrong choice when only one clustering exists and no labels are available, because a score then has nothing to be read against. The external indices need ground-truth labels.

technique: Repeated-run consistency test (test-retest; intra-coder reliability; TARr@N and TARa@N (raw and parsed answer agreement); settings pinning)
what_it_does: Runs the same prompt and input N times, with model version, temperature and seed fixed and recorded, and measures agreement. Artefact: agreement rates and accuracy spread. Read both the spread and whether outputs are identical strings.
fit_test: Use for any LLM step on which a conclusion depends. Misfit: only one run exists. Pinning settings reduces variance but does not remove it.
status_and_evidence: Tested. Across five LLMs, eight tasks and ten runs each, accuracy varied by up to 15 per cent between runs, the best-to-worst gap reached 70 per cent, and no model was consistent on all tasks (2024). ([Atil et al. 2024, arXiv 2408.04667](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04667); [Reiss, arXiv 2304.11085](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11085))
purpose: Run the same prompt and input several times with model version, temperature and seed recorded, and produce agreement rates and accuracy spread in a validation report.
use_when: Use when a conclusion depends on a language model step and you need to know whether it gives the same answer each time.
requires_minimum: at least 5 repeated runs on a sample of items
not_for_text: Wrong choice when only one run exists and none can be made. Pinning settings reduces variance but does not remove it, and stable output is not correct output.
related_techniques: should follow :: MM-08 :: the model coding step is what gets repeated; pairs with :: CK-11 :: prompt paraphrases test a different source of instability; pairs with :: CK-12 :: a specification sweep shows downstream effects of instability
typical_model_failure: Reports a single run as the result, or assumes temperature 0 gives identical output.

output_spec: The result gives the number of runs, the fixed and recorded model version, temperature and seed, the agreement rate across runs and the spread in accuracy. It also states whether the outputs were identical strings.

technique: Prompt stability scoring (prompt perturbation; paraphrase test)
what_it_does: Re-runs the task with paraphrased prompts and applies reliability metrics to the labels. Artefact: a stability score. Read it before scaling a classification prompt to a large corpus.
fit_test: Fits a classification prompt that will be used on a large corpus. Misfit: paraphrases that differ in substance. The paraphrase set defines what counts as a small change.
status_and_evidence: Tested. A prompt stability score was tested on about 3.1 million rows across six datasets and twelve outcomes (2024); the scores were not on the abstract page. ([Barrie, Palaiologou and Tornberg 2024, arXiv 2407.02039](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.02039))
purpose: Re-run a task with paraphrased prompts and apply reliability metrics to the labels, and produce a prompt stability score in a validation report.
use_when: Use when a classification prompt will be applied to a large corpus and you need to know whether wording changes the labels.
requires_minimum: at least 5 paraphrased prompts and a sample of items to label under each
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the paraphrases differ in substance, because the paraphrase set defines what counts as a small change.
related_techniques: should follow :: MM-08 :: the prompt under test comes from the coding step; pairs with :: CK-10 :: repeated runs test stability across runs and not across wording; pairs with :: CK-12 :: a specification sweep shows downstream effects of prompt choice
typical_model_failure: Results change with the wording and nobody notices.

error_sources: input data; language model
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when labels change across paraphrases (inconsistency) and when the paraphrase set is narrow (indirectness).

technique: Specification sweep across models and prompts (LLM hacking test; multiverse analysis; specification curve)
what_it_does: Repeats the downstream statistical test across several models, prompts and settings and reports the share of conclusions that change. Artefact: error rates for false positive, false negative, wrong-sign and wrong-magnitude conclusions. Read results near a significance threshold with extra care.
fit_test: Use for any significance claim built on LLM labels. The multiverse and specification curve names are general knowledge and were not confirmed.
status_and_evidence: Tested. Across 13 million labels from 18 LLMs and 2,361 hypotheses, about 31 per cent of hypotheses reached incorrect conclusions with state-of-the-art models and about half with smaller models. A few prompt paraphrases made nearly any result significant, and human annotations were the most important of 21 safeguards (2025 preprint). ([Baumann et al. 2025, arXiv 2509.08825](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08825))

not_for_text: Wrong choice when error types overlap, so that counts do not add up. Types must be defined before counting.
related_techniques: should follow :: CK-24 :: the sampled and reviewed items supply the failures; should follow :: CK-26 :: reviewer decisions supply the failures; pairs with :: CK-27 :: adversarial failures can be classified with the same taxonomy

error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when types overlap (indirectness), when few failures were reviewed (imprecision) and when one reviewer classified them (risk of bias).

technique: Independent human review of model output (expert review; adjudication; human oversight)
what_it_does: Specifies who reviews which outputs, with what rubric and with authority to overrule. Artefact: a review log with decisions. Read the overruled items and the reasons.
fit_test: Fits any output used in a decision. Misfit: reviewers see only items the model approved (automation bias, inference). Neither source gives sample sizes or reviewer numbers.
status_and_evidence: Documented. NIST says reviewers should not be directly involved in developing the same model and that review should be prioritised by risk. The Australian standard asks for a competent person with authority to intervene. ([NIST AI 600-1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf); [Voluntary AI Safety Standard, 10 guardrails](https://www.industry.gov.au/publications/voluntary-ai-safety-standard/10-guardrails))
purpose: Specify who reviews which outputs, with what rubric and with authority to overrule, and produce a review log with decisions.
use_when: Use when an output will inform a decision and a person who did not build it must check and be able to overrule it.
requires_minimum: at least one reviewer who did not develop the model, and a written rubric
not_for_text: Wrong choice when reviewers see only the items the model approved, which invites automation bias. Neither source gives sample sizes or reviewer numbers.
related_techniques: should follow :: CK-24 :: the sample design says which items reviewers see; pairs with :: CK-25 :: reviewed failures are classified; should follow :: family:Prepare and extract :: the extracted outputs are what reviewers check
typical_model_failure: Reports "reviewed" when no reviewer saw the output.
minimum_checks: exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:human review sample; decision-informing:provenance log; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:provenance log; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:expert review
error_sources: input data; coder or rater judgement; expert opinion
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when reviewers see only approved items (risk of bias), when review is rushed (imprecision) and when reviewers lack subject knowledge (indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a review log with one row per output reviewed, giving the reviewer, the rubric applied, the decision and the reason. It states who reviews which outputs and lists the overruled items with the reasons.

technique: Adversarial testing of an extraction pipeline (red-teaming; chaos testing)
what_it_does: Probes the pipeline with hostile or odd inputs, such as instructions inserted in source text, contradictory documents and missing data. Artefact: a list of failures found. Read the failures that change a reported result.
fit_test: Fits pipelines that handle untrusted documents. Misfit: the testers also built the system. Both sources aim at safety and security more than analytic accuracy (inference).
status_and_evidence: Documented. NIST AI 600-1 calls for red-teaming, and the Australian guardrail 4 includes it for general-purpose AI. ([NIST AI 600-1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf); [Voluntary AI Safety Standard, 10 guardrails](https://www.industry.gov.au/publications/voluntary-ai-safety-standard/10-guardrails))
purpose: Probe an extraction pipeline with hostile or odd inputs such as instructions inserted in source text, contradictory documents and missing data, and produce a list of failures found.
use_when: Use when a pipeline reads documents from outside sources and you need to know whether planted or odd content can change its output.
requires_minimum: a runnable pipeline and a set of test inputs written by someone other than its builder
not_for_text: Wrong choice when the testers also built the system. Both guidance sources aim at safety and security more than analytic accuracy.
related_techniques: should follow :: PE-10 :: structured extraction is exposed to inserted instructions; should follow :: PE-13 :: retrieved passages can carry inserted instructions; pairs with :: CK-25 :: failures found are classified by type
typical_model_failure: Follows instructions embedded in source documents.

error_sources: input data; language model; expert opinion
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when testers also built the pipeline (risk of bias) and when test inputs cover only known attack types (indirectness).

output_spec: The result is a list of the failures found, each with the hostile or odd input that caused it, such as inserted instructions, contradictory documents or missing data. It marks which failures change a reported result.

technique: Provenance tracking and audit logging (W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) PROV; lineage; record keeping)
what_it_does: Records which source, prompt, model version, settings, reviewer and decision produced each output, as a graph of entities, activities and agents. Artefact: a provenance graph or log. Read the derivation chain to find whether two sources trace to one origin, and to retrace any claim to its source.
fit_test: Fits when derivation links can be recorded as they happen. Misfit: provenance is missing or added afterwards. PROV records provenance but does not judge reliability. NIST and the Australian standard require record keeping for tests and results, and give no field list.
status_and_evidence: Documented. PROV describes provenance as information about the entities, activities and people involved in producing data, used to judge quality and reliability. ([W3C PROV overview](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/); [W3C PROV-DM](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/); [W3C PROV-O](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/); [NIST AI 600-1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf); [Voluntary AI Safety Standard, 10 guardrails](https://www.industry.gov.au/publications/voluntary-ai-safety-standard/10-guardrails))
purpose: Record which source, prompt, model version, settings, reviewer and decision produced each output, and produce a provenance graph or log that traces any claim back to its source.
use_when: Use when you must retrace a claim to its source, show how an output was made, or find whether two sources trace to one origin.
other_phases: verify and prepare; analyse; validate; report
requires_minimum: derivation links recorded as work happens
not_for_text: Wrong choice when provenance is missing or added afterwards. A provenance record does not judge reliability, and no source gives a field list.
related_techniques: pairs with :: IS-06 :: derivation chains show whether sources share an origin; pairs with :: CK-29 :: a scripted workflow records code and environment alongside provenance
typical_model_failure: Infers a derivation link from similar wording that was never recorded, writes a plausible reconstructed account of its steps instead of logging real ones, or treats same-origin sources as independent.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:provenance log; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:provenance log; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; data transformation
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when links were reconstructed afterwards (risk of bias) and when recorded steps are incomplete (indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a provenance graph or log that links each output to the source, prompt, model version, settings, reviewer and decision that produced it, as entities, activities and agents. It states whether any two sources trace to one origin and shows the derivation chain from a claim back to its source.

technique: Scripted reproducible workflow (reproducible analysis; version control; literate programming)
what_it_does: Records data, code and environment so that another person or a later run can regenerate every figure. Artefact: a project directory with raw data, scripts, a dependency list and test data. Read whether the outputs can be regenerated from the raw data by running the scripts.
fit_test: A fresh run from raw data reproduces the results. Misfit: manual spreadsheet edits or untracked cleaning steps. Reproducing a number does not show it is correct.
status_and_evidence: Practice. Practitioner recommendations published by researchers: keep raw data read-only, use tidy data, script every processing step, make dependencies explicit and use version control. ([Good enough practices in scientific computing](https://swcarpentry.github.io/good-enough-practices-in-scientific-computing))
purpose: Record data, code and environment so that another person or a later run can regenerate every figure, and produce a project record that can be rerun from the raw data.
use_when: Use when results must be reproducible by someone else or by a later run from the raw data.
requires_minimum: raw data kept read-only and every processing step scripted
not_for_text: Wrong choice when cleaning was done by manual spreadsheet edits that cannot be scripted. Reproducing a number does not show that it is correct.
related_techniques: pairs with :: CK-28 :: provenance records which source and decision produced each output
typical_model_failure: Reports a result without the script that produced it, so it cannot be rerun.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:provenance log; decision-informing:spot check; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:provenance log; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; data transformation
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when any step was done by hand (risk of bias) and when the environment was not recorded (indirectness).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result describes a project directory holding the raw data, the scripts, a dependency list and test data. It states whether the outputs were regenerated from the raw data by running the scripts and lists any step that could not be regenerated.

technique: De-identification and re-identification risk assessment (data situation audit; direct and indirect identifier removal; disclosure risk assessment)
what_it_does: Removes or alters identifying details and assesses whether a person could still be identified once the data are released or analysed in context. Artefact: a de-identified dataset and a short re-identification risk statement. Read the risk in the context of who will see the output and what other data they hold.
fit_test: Does the material hold personal or sensitive information that the analysis, sharing or model use does not need? If yes, run this before any other technique.
status_and_evidence: Documented. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) states that removing direct identifiers alone may not de-identify data under the Privacy Act and that re-identification risk must be assessed in context. The OAIC and CSIRO Data61 De-identification Decision-Making Framework has three activities: a data situation audit, risk analysis and control, and impact management. ([OAIC, De-identification and the Privacy Act](https://oaic.gov.au/privacy/guidance-and-advice/de-identification-and-the-privacy-act); [OAIC, De-identification Decision-Making Framework](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/guidance-and-advice/de-identification-decision-making-framework/))
purpose: Removes or alters identifying details and assesses the risk that a person can still be identified in the context of release, giving a de-identified dataset and a re-identification risk statement.
use_when: Use when material holds personal or sensitive information and the analysis, sharing or model use needs it removed or reduced first.
requires_minimum: The intended use of the output, the people who will see it, and a list of other data that could be linked to it.
not_for_text: Removing direct identifiers such as names and addresses is read as de-identification, and complex or publicly released datasets still need specialist advice.
related_techniques: pairs with :: PE-08 :: named entity recognition finds the names and places to remove; pairs with :: PE-04 :: profiling shows which fields could identify a person
typical_model_failure: Removes names and addresses and declares the data de-identified, although the remaining details in combination can still identify a person.
minimum_checks: exploratory:input validation; exploratory:spot check; decision-informing:input validation; decision-informing:spot check; decision-informing:human review sample; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:input validation; high-stakes:spot check; high-stakes:human review sample; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:independent review; high-stakes:expert review
error_sources: input data; data transformation; language model
certainty_limits: Certainty that the data are de-identified drops when other datasets could be linked in (indirectness) and when the context of release is not known.
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result has a de-identified dataset and a short re-identification risk statement. The statement names the identifiers removed or altered, who will see the output and what other data they hold, and gives the risk judged in that context.

technique: Ranking uncertainty analysis (stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis; SMAA; rank acceptability index)
what_it_does: Samples criteria weights and score uncertainty many times and counts how often each option takes each rank. Artefact: rank acceptability indices and central weights per option. Read them as how far the ranking depends on the assumed weights and scores, not as the chance that an option is best.
fit_test: Have the options already been scored on weighted criteria, and does the decision depend on whether the ranking would survive different weights? If yes, use this after the scoring.
status_and_evidence: Documented. SMAA is a published family of methods for multi-criteria decision problems with uncertain or missing information, with rank acceptability indices, central weights and confidence factors as outputs. ([Lahdelma and Salminen, SMAA chapter abstract](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:spr:isochp:978-1-4419-5904-1_10); [CRAN smaa package manual](https://cran.r-universe.dev/smaa/doc/manual.html))
purpose: Samples weights and score uncertainty many times and reports how often each option takes each rank, giving rank acceptability indices that show how stable a multi-criteria ranking is.
use_when: Use when options have been scored against weighted criteria, or the material supplies scores and weights, and the decision depends on how stable the ranking is.
requires_minimum: At least two options, scores on at least two criteria, and a range or distribution for each score or weight.
not_for_text: Rank shares are read as the chance that an option is truly best; they show only how the ranking responds to the assumed uncertainty.
consumes: charter or question:agreed; raw dataset or corpus:raw
related_techniques: pairs with :: AO-12 :: multi-criteria scoring and ranking uncertainty read the same scores and weights, and the second shows how stable the first ranking is; pairs with :: TC1-17 :: sensitivity analysis varies one input at a time while this technique varies all weights together
typical_model_failure: Samples weights evenly across the whole range, so an extreme weight on one criterion is treated as likely as a balanced set, and then reports the share of samples as a probability.
minimum_checks: exploratory:assumption and limitation statement; exploratory:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:assumption and limitation statement; decision-informing:code execution for arithmetic; decision-informing:repeat runs; decision-informing:sensitivity analysis; high-stakes:assumption and limitation statement; high-stakes:code execution for arithmetic; high-stakes:repeat runs; high-stakes:sensitivity analysis; high-stakes:second technique with different assumptions; high-stakes:independent review
error_sources: input data; statistical assumptions; expert opinion
certainty_limits: Certainty drops when scores come from one rater (risk of bias) and when the weight ranges were set without agreement (imprecision).
tag_basis: input profile inference; selection inference; sequencing inference; robustness inference
output_spec: The result is a table with one row per option, giving the rank acceptability index for each rank and the central weights. It states how far the ranking depends on the assumed weights and scores, and does not describe the index as the chance that an option is best.
